THE WAR-TRAIL. A ROMANCE. BY CAPTAIN MAYNE REID. CHAPTER LXXXIV. ' PAINTING INJUN.' Withal, I was not reckless. If not sanguine, was far from despondent ; and as I continued to dwell upon it, tbe prospect seemed to brighten, and success to appear less problematical. One of the chief difficulties I should have to encounter would be getting into camp. Once inside the lines þÿ that is, among the camp-fires and tents, if there should be any þÿ I would be comparatively safe. This I knew from experience ; for it would not be nty first visit to an encampment of prairie-lndians. Even in their midst, mingling with the savages themselves, and under the light of their glaring fires, I should be less exposed to the danger of detection than while attempting to cross their lines. First, there might be outlying pickets ; then within these the horse-guards; and within these, again, the horses themselves ! You may smile, when I assert that the last was to me a source of apprehension as great as either of the others. An Indian horse is a sen- I tinel not to be despised. He is as much the enemy of the whiteman as his master ; and j partly from fear, and partly from actual antipathy, he will not permit the former to approach him. The human watcher may be negligentmay sleep upon his post þÿ the mustang never. The scent of a white man, or the sight of a skulking form, will cause him to snort and neigh ; | so that a whole camp will either be stampeded or put upon the alert in a few minutes. Many a well-planned attack has been defeated by the j !

warning-snort of the sentinel horse. | It is not that the prairie-horse feels any pecu- 1 liar attachment for the Indian ; strange if lie did þÿ since tyrant more cruel to the equine race does not exist þÿ no driver more severe, no rider more bard than a horse-Indian. It is simply the faithfulness which the noble animal exhibits lor his companion and master, with the instinct which tills him when that mas- | ter is menaced by danger. He will do the same service for a white as for a red man ; and ofteu j does the weary trapper take his lone rest with full confidence that the vigil will be faithfully kept by his horse. Had there been dogs in the Indian camp, my apprehensions would have been still more acute j -the danger would have been more than doubled. Even within the lines, these cunning brutes would have known me as an enemy : the disguise of garments would not avail ; by the sccut, an Indian dog can at ouce tell the white from the red man ; and they appear to hold a real antipathy against the race of the Saxon. Even in time of truce, a white man entering an Indian camp can scarcely he protected from the wolfish pack. I knew there were no dogs þÿ of none. The Indians had been upon the. wartrail ; and when they proceed on these grand expeditions their dogs, like their women, are left þÿ at þÿhome. I had reason to be thankful that such was their custom. Of course it was my intention to go disguised ; it would have been madness to have gone otherwise. In the darkest night, my uniform would

have betrayed me ; but necessarily, in my search for the captive, I should be led within the light of the fires. It was my design, therefore, to counterfeit the Indian costume ; and how to do this had been for some time the subject of my reflections. I had been congratulating myself on the possession of the buffalo-robe That would go far towards the disguise ; but other articles were wanting to complete my costume. The leggings and moccasins þÿ the plumed head-dress and neck ornaments, the long straggling locks, the bronze complexion of arms and breastþÿ the piebald face of chalk, charcoal, and vermilion þÿ where were all these to he obtained ? There was no eostumerie in the desert. In tho moment of excitement that succeeded the capture of the savage, I had been thinking of other things. It was only when we were about to part from him that the idea jumped into my mind þÿ that bright þÿidea that he could fnrnish þÿme the very man. I turned back to reconnoitre his person. Dismounting, I scanned hint from head to foot

It was a grim smile, however, and from the first moment to the last, neither word nor ejaculation escaped from his lips.

Even I was forced to smile ; I could not restrain myself. The odd travesty in which we were engaged þÿ tbe strange commiugliug of tho comic and serious iu tho act þÿ and above all, the ludicrous look of the captive Indian, after they had close cropped him, was enough to make a stone smile. THE EAST 1IUVRS ON TUB TRAIL More cautiously than ever, we now crept along the trail, advancing only after the ground had been thoroughly þÿ quartered bv the scouts. Time was of the least consequence The flesh sigu of the Indians told us they were but a short way ahead of us : we could have ridden within sight of them at any moment. We did not wish to set eyes on tin m before sunset. It could be no advantage to us to overtake them on the march, hut the contrary. Some lagging Iudiau might he found in the rear of the band; we might come in contact with him, and thus defeat all our designs. We hung back, therefore, allowing time for the savages to pitch their camp, and for their stragglers to get into it.

Ou the other hand, I did not desire to arrive late. The council was to be held that night þÿ so she had learned þÿ and after the council would come the crisis. T must be in time for both. At what hour would the council take place ? It might he just after they had halted. The sou of a chief, and a chief himselfþÿ for the white renegade was a leader of red men þÿ a question between two such men would not remain lone: undecided. And a question of so mueli importance-involving þÿ in body and soul possession of the most beauti- such consequence þÿ property ful woman iu tho world ! Oh I I wondered! Could these hideous, ochre-stained, grease-bedaubed brutes appreciate that peerless beauty? Impossible, I thought The delicate lines of her loveliness would be lost upon their gross eyes and coarse sensual hearts. That pearl beyond price þÿ paste would have satisfied them as well þÿ they could not distinguish tho diamond from common class. And yet the Comanche is not without lovecraft. Coarse as might be the passion, they must have loved þÿher both must have loved her þÿ red savage and white savage. For this very re .son, the þÿ þÿtrial would not he delayed; the question would be speedily decided, so that the quarrel of the chiefs might be brought to an end. For this very reason, the crisis might be hastened, the council take place at an early hour ; for this very reason, I too must needs be upon the spot at an early hour. It was my aim to arrive within sight of the Indian encampment just before night þÿ in tho

twilight, if possible þÿ that wc might he able to make reconnaissance of the ground before darkness would cover it from our view. WTe were desirous of acquainting ourselves with the lay of the surrounding country as well, so that, in tho event of our escape, we should know which was the best direction to take. We timed our advance by the sign upon tho trail. The keen scouts could tell, almost to a minute, when the latest tracks were made ; and by this we were guided Both glided silently along, their eyes constantly and earnestly turned upon the ground. Mine were more anxiously bent upon the sky; from that quarter I most feared an obstacle to tho execution of my purposo. What a chango had come over my desires ! þÿ how different were they from those of tho two preceding nights 1 The very same aspect of the heavens that had hitherto chagrined and baffled tr.e, would now have been welcome. In my heart, I bad lately oxecrated the cloud-; in that same heart T was now praying for cloud, and storm, and daikueas ! To be continued

Trinity Bay, August 5. To the Associate, l Press , New York : The Atlantic Telegraph fleet sailed from Queens-town, on Saturday, July 17th, met at mid-ocean on Wednesday the 28th, made the splice at 1 P. M. on Thursday, the 29th, and then separated, the Agamemnon and the Valorous bound to Valencia, Ireland, and the Niagara and Gorgon for this place, where they arrived yesterday, and this morning the end of the cable will be landed. It is sixteen hundred and ninety-eight nautical, or nineteen hundred and fifty statute miles from the Telegraph House at the head of Valencia Harbor to the Telegraph House, Bay of Bulls, Trinity Bay ; and for more than two-thirds of this distance the water is over two miles in depth. The cable has been paid out from the Agamemnon at about the same speed as from the Niagara. The electrical signals sent and received through the whole cable are perfect. The machinery for p.iyiug out the cable worked in the most satisfactory manner, and was not stopped for a single moment from the time the splice was made until we arrived here. Captain Hudson, Messrs. Everett and Woodhouse, the engineers, the electricians and others of the ships and in fact every man on board the telegraph fleet, has exerted himself to the utmost to make the expedition successful!, and by the blessing of Divine Providence it has been successful. After the end of the cable islanded and con nected with the land line of Telegraph, and the Niagara has discharged some cargo belonging
to the Telegraph Uempany, she will go to St. Johns for coals, and then proceed at once to New York. CYRUS W. FIELD.

Ocean Telegraphs. þÿ From Falmouth to Gibraltar the distance is less than 1,000 miles ; from Gibraltar to Malta the distance is 988 miles; from Malta to Alexandria it is 816 miles; from Suez to Aden, 1,810 miles; from Aden to Bombay, 1,664 miles; from Bombay to Foin de Galle 960 miles from Point de Guile to Madras, 540 miles; from Madras to Calcutta, 780 miles ; from Calcutta to Penang, 1,213 miles ; from Peuang to Singapore, 381 miles ; from Singapore to llong Kong, 1,437 miles; from Siugapore to Batavia, 520 miles ; from Batavia to Swan River 1,500 miles; from Swan River to King George's Sound, 500 miles ; and from King George's Sound to Adelaide, 998 miles. From Adelaide to Melbourne and Sydney there will shortly be a telegraphic communication overland. From Trinity Bay, in Newfoundland, to Bermuda, the distance is 1,500 miles ; from Bermuda to Inagua the distance is about 1,000 miles; from Inagua to Jamaica it is 300 miles; from Jamaica to Antigua, 800 miles ; from Antigua to Demerara, via Trinidad, 800 miles ; from Antigua to St. Thomas, 227 miles; from Jamaica to Greytown, via Navy Bay, 1,000 miles; and from Jamaica to Belize, 700 miles. It will be thus seen that all our settlements, dependencies and colonies in the Peninsula, Mediterranean, Arabia, India, China, Australia, the West Indies and Central America, could be joined to England by shorter submarine cables than that which at present connect Ireland with Newfoundland, and without their touching any powerful foreign State.

The aggregate length of these cables would be about 21,000 miles, and reckoning 20 per cent, for slack, the whole length would not measure more than 24,000 miles. These cables would place England in almost instantaneous communication with upwards of forty colonics, settlements and dependencies situated 20,000 miles apart, in the eastern and western hemispheres. A Novel Steam-ship. þÿ There is now in West Hartlepool a steam-ship of a novel and peculiar construction which has attracted the attention of large numbers both of scientific and non-scientific spectators. The vessel, which is built of iron, is in three separate moveable compartments which fit together like socketjoints, and arc held in position by powerful iron longitudinal stays. The vessel is about 90 feet in length and nine in breadth, a very narrow beam. Her engine is placed in the aftermost section, and the foremost one is ocposes. cupied by the crew, and used consists The central portion for the usual pur- of the hold only, and which may be completely disconnected from the other portion in a few minutes. The steamer is intended to load coal for the London market, and is. we understand, simply an experimental vessel, for tlie purpose of test ing the practicability of the inventor's scheme, which is that of having a vessel so constructed that, if a speedy sale cannot be effected, the portion of the vessel containing the cargo may bo disconnected and left behind till market day, its place being filled by an empty portion
with which the vessel can proceed immediately for another cargo. The steamer is appropriately named the Connector, and will carry Between 30 and 40 tons of coal.

Who Invented the Electric Telegraph. To the Editor of the Ne o York Tribune Sir : In the Tribune of yesterday I find reported a speech of Gov. Seward at Auburn, in which is the following passage : þÿ It was a citizen of New York who resumed the task of taming the lightning where Frank lin had left þÿit. This is incorrect ; and as a countryman of Hans Christian Oersted, I cannot let such a statement pass without a few remarks, especially þÿ cannot fail to add considerably to an idea in as it þÿ coming from such a high authority the United States prevalent, that the electromagnetic telegraph is wholly duo to Benjamin Franklin and Samuel F. B. Morse. Permit me, therefore, through your valuable organ, to state that, without the intervening discoveries of that great Dane þÿ who was professor in physical science at the University of Copenhagen þÿ we should most þÿlikely never have heard of an electro-magnetic telegraph, for it was Oersted who discovered the principles of electro-magnetism, or in other words, for conducting voltaic currents, and this discovery was reached, not like most of other discoveries, by a chance þÿ it was a result of profound philosophy. Benjamin Franklin was a respectable contemplator of nature, nnd Professor Morse is an ingenious inventor, hut Oersted was a king among men of science, and it is mainly to him that we arc indebted for that wondrous thought carrier, an electro-magnetic telegraph. Respectfully yours C. F. RAUN. Poughkeepsie, Aug. 15, 1858. o From the ll'cst Indian. Ilarbados, Sejil. 3, 158.

The Screw Steam Ship Mauritius witli the Chinese Emigrants, left Carlisle Bay tins forenoon for her destination, Havana, where wo wish her passengers may find more comfortable quarters, than from what we read of the Sugar Estates of Culm, upon wflich they are to he located, wo anticipate for them. Tie re are 685 Chinamen fiom Canton onboard, nnd a strange appearance they make, crowded together on the deck of the Mauritius, with large round straw hats on and brown calico clothes. They appear cheerful and satisfied with the treatment they have received on hoard They are docile and peaceable, and the Captain, Mr. Cruikshank, we are informed, says that lie has experienced no difficulty in keeping order amongst them A few of them were permitted to come on shore and take a peep at Bridgetown. \Ye learn that the Mauritius was visited by His Excellency the Governor, who satisfied himself of the condition of the Emigrants, and that they were apprised of the true character of the contract into which they had entered, which appears to he to wrk on the Estates for four dollars a month, and their hoard and lodging. Considering the groat length of the voyage, 102 days, and the number of Emigrants, the deaths on hoard, about 50, do not exceed the average mortality in ships of this kind ; and if there was any guarantee for their kind treatment in Cuba after the expiration of their contract, and the fulfilment of its terms on the part of their employers, þÿ which the Cuban Government perhaps will enforce, just ns tlie

British Government does with respect to the Coolie Immigrants in Guiana nnd Trinidad, we sec nothing to find fault of hut the contrary, in the employment of these vessels, which are amongst the finest in the Mercantile Navy of Great Britain, to convey the redundant laborers of China to the West Indies, and even to Cuba, a Foreign Slave Colony, and the great rival of the British West Indies, in the supply of the markets of the world with sugar. We are inclined to believe that the introduction of free labor will help to depreciate and to banish slave labor in Cuba, and if the Cuban Planters could get a sufficient number of free laborers either amongst the resident population, or by immigration from India, China and elsewhere, they would find it to their as interest to abandon the African Slave Trade, has happened in

þÿBran ll. It is said that the condition of the lower class of Chinese, in their own country, is such that it can scarcely be conceived to be worse in Cuba or anywhere else. They emigrate in large numbers to the Islands in the Eastern Seas, and to Australia, from where we see it proposed to keep them away by legal enactment, as has been done in California. Th y are an industrious ingenious and frugal people, and club together, on account of ceremo- and their strange habits and religious which nies they seem to incur the jealousy and dislike of European settlers in the gold countries. In A ustrali i and California they are becoming so numerous as to create apprehensions of the future growth of an element in the population alien in blood religion and morals from the prevailing race, which has led in the latter State to the passing of an Act of the Legislature to forbid the introduction of any more of the pig þÿtai s. An mug t the emigrants on board the Mauritius, is an historical personage, Commissioner þÿYci s executioner, who could st:ike off 30 heads in a minute, who as it appears by an advertisement of Mr. Man, the Photographist, was brought on shore yesterday by the officers of the ship, to have his likeness taken. It appears, after þÿYea s capture, fearing the vengeance. of the populace, lie joined the emigrants on board the Mauritius. Mr. Man says lie is a man ot particularly mild couutenancc and disposition ; and lie has not only his photograph, but his þÿpig t s ail, for which ho gave him 2s. Gd.

We understand there arc two other First Class Ships, on their way by this from Canton, with Immigrants for the Havana, following the Mauritius, to coal at Barbados : which shows the advantage of the position of this Island, and how great an object is the enlargement of the Port, to make Barbados a place of call for the accommodation of Vessels from the East Indies and from Brazil, on their way to the Gull of Mexico, and the Coasts of North America þÿ a traffic which is þÿdaily increasing. We nave heard it said that the time is coming when a Vessel of even the size of the Mauritius, will enter the Careenage, and find accommodation there, whether it is for coal and water, or for repairs ; that there is nothing impossible nor impracticable in the idea, and that its accomplishment is merely a work of time. We are hardly so sanguine ; but it is plain to all that much can he done for the improvement of our Port þÿ how much we do not stop to enquire þÿ and the sooner it is done the better. The Mauritius spent 300 dollars every day, whilst lying h -re, and was an object of great curiosity at a distance of half a mile ; how much more would she have excited the curiosity of every one had she come closer, and laid alongside the Wharves of the City.

CHRISTIANSTED, ST. CROIX. TUESDAY, 2 1 st SEPTEMBER, 185S. We confess to have felt some surprise at the Success of the concert held in St. þÿJohn Church s last evening. We did not go to hear professional Singers ; Dor yet did we anticipate such good singing from voices which have received so small a degree of training. We cannot say, as many have perhaps said, that the singing was as well as we could expect ; we feel ourselves rather compelled to declare that it was better than we expected. It would be difficult to find others, with similar small advantages, to till the places of those who so disinterestedly applied their native talents to such a charitable purpose. Baron dc Fleur performed on the Harmonium and Piano Forte at the same time, and executed some fine pieces during the evening. Ti e Concert will be repeated on Thursday next for the accommodation of those who could not obtain seats last evening.

SPAIN. Tho Discusion contains an article strongly recommending the Government to make war on Morocco, in order to put down definitively the pirates of the Riff, and to obtain a tract of territory which shall enable it to found a large and fertile colony. For some time past journals of provincial towns near the Mediterranean have been recommending the same thing. A report from a gentleman who lately visited tho African coast is published in one of the Madrid papers. It says that the fertility of that coast is remarkable ; that the inhabitants are much higher in the social scale than is generally supposed, and that there appears to be little or no feeling of hostility among them to the Spaniards It then goes on to assert that the conquest of part of Morocco would be comparatively easy for Spain, especially at the present time, when civil war is raging in that country, and when the Emperor finds it difficult to reduce to his sway the tribes that have risen in insurrection. A letter says þÿ þÿ The Queen lias declared her intentiou of founding nine great asylums tor the the poor, one for each archbishopric in tlm kingdom. In consequence, mendicity, which has become one of the plagues of the country, is to he suppressed everywhere from the 1st of next October, and the poor are to bo sent to the asylums, receiving relief on their way from the municipalities. 9,000,000 reals are to be employed towards defraying the expenses of these asylums, and the Queen proposes to make up the rest of the money neces-

sary by means of appeals to public charity. Among the edifices to be set apart for the asylums arc the Escurial and the famous San Mar tin de Santiago. In the asylums children arc to be taught useful trades, and employment is to be found for adults. The alms distributed iu the province of Leon hy the Queen exceed $7,000. Her Majesty has made the statue of the Virgin at Mercado an offering of a pair of diamond ear-rings, and other ornaments of great value. þÿ Flic Queen has likewise promised to send a mantle to our Blessed Lady of the Roads (Nucstra Sonora dc los Cmniuos) at Leon, and a gold chalice to the bishop of the | þÿdiocese. The Constitutionncl gives the following semiofficial account of the result of the Paris Conferences relative to the Dauubian Principalities: þÿ þÿ The Conference charged witli the organisa tion of the Principalities has finished its task

after three months of laborious sittings. But the result of its labours will, as has been announced, only be published when the ratifications have been exchanged. Meantime we are enabled to give a brief summary of the more important points of the new organisation. under- fundamental principle of the union, as The stood by France, has not prevailed. This is a result which might easily have been foreseen, as the views of the majority of the signing Powers were well known. But if the Governuent of the Emperor has not obtained what it lesired, and what it still maintains to be the icst bads for the new state of things, that is to say a complete union, it nevertheless appears that what has been done is a step towards that union, and even that the new organisation sanctions it and realises it in many respects. The two Principalities, if we arc well informed, will receive perfectly identical political institutions, and this identity prevails throughout. Thus, equality before the law, taxation, personal liberty, property, privileges of caste, admission to public employment, are identical in both Principalities. A sort of Council of State, permanent and common to both Principalities, is invested with considerable powers, especially as regards the institution of laws. This Council will be nominated by the llospodars and Assemblies of the. two Principalities. A High Court of Justice and of Appeal, the members of which will be appointed for life, will be instituted in common for both Principalities.

As regards the Elective Assemblies, each Principality will have its own, elected, not by universal suffrage, but according to a fixed census. These Assemblies will have an important part in the mechanism of the Government. For instance, they will elect the Hospodars, hitherto appointed by the Porte. They will be selected by the Assembly of each Principality, bound under certain conditions of candidateship determined by the Convention. The Sublime Porte will simply perform the act of in vesture of the llospodars No act of the Hospodar will be valid unless countersigned by a Minister. The responsibility of the Ministers towards the Legislative Chambers is clearly I and severely defined, and these Chambers will possess a serious control. The question of the corvces has also beeu þÿconsidered. The Paris correspondent of the 7'imcs, in a letter dated Sunday evening, says : þÿ þÿ does It not appear that the increased mildness of administration we were told to expect from the present Minister of the Interior is carried to the length of preserving Frenchmen from arbitrary deportation for political causes. I am assured by a highly trustworthy person that, at Toulon, on or about the 30th of last month, he saw 20 persons, escorted by the gendarmerie and the police of the town, conducted to the military port, and coming apparently from the fort of La Malgue. After passing some hours in the bagnio, they were taken out to the roads and embarked on board the Eclaireur, which conveyed them to Marseilles in the bound placed them on board the Yonnc, night and for

Brest with a steam-engine of 600-horse power, intended for one of the vessels in the last-named port. To Brest these 20 prisoners w of veyed, there to form part of a convoy galley ere conslaves for Cayenne It is also certain that the 20 persons in question were condemned to be transported to Cayenne by administrative measure (in virtue of the new Law of Public Safety), after having undergone certain punishments as vagabonds, members of secret societies, Ac. Among them was M. Delccluze, former Prelect of the Department of the Nord under the Republic. It is not known whether his companions in captivity had been punished for political or for sonic other offence. M. Dclecluze, however, had been condemned for political causes ; and when the term of his punishment was over he was informed that he had been pronounced dangerous by a commission composed of the Prefect, of the General of the District and of the Procureur Imperial, and that, he would be sent to Cayenne. Meanwhile lie was committed to Fort La Malgue, at Toulon. PRUSSIA A letter from Berlin says : þÿ þÿ A police order prohibiting the newspapers from alluding to the deliberations of the Council of Ministers has produced a great sensation here. The prohibition is attributed to important discussions which are about to take place in the Council respecting the Regency. It seems certain that the Prince of Prussia will soon definitively assume the r. ins of Government, and that the Ministry will be greatly modified, if not entirely changed. Thu leaders of the Conservative party go successively to Tcgerusee to pay their respects to the King. It has been decided that Prussian Consuls shall be established at Nicholaieff, at the mouth of the Amoor, in the island of Candia, and in the kingdom of þÿSiam. A correspondent of the lndependance litlgc, writing from Berlin, states that for some weeks past the physicians have interdicted the Princess Frederick William from taking railway journeys, her accouchement being expected in October. The so-called þÿ Criminal þÿSenate of the Court of Appeals in Stettin, has just given judgment in the case of the seven Danish captains accused of infringing the Prussian laws relative to the coasting trade, by bringing eargoes of grain from Dantzic to this town. It will bo remembered that, about a month ago, the Ordinary Tribunal acquitted the captains iu the first instance, and that the. State Procurator protested against the d eision. and submitted the case to the Court of Appeals. The latter has now reversed the judgment pro-

nounced by the inferior Court, sentences the ships and their cargoes to confiscation to the Crown, and orders the Danish owners to pay the costs both of the original trial and that of the Court of Appeals. AUSTRIA. A conspiracy was discovered some time since at Lemberg, the capital of Austrian Galicia. It originated in one of the schools here, most of the conspirators being from 12 to 15years of age. Eleven of them have been tried and sentenced, one to death, and the others to various terms of imprisonment. In passing sentence the Judges themselves recommended them to mercy, on account of their extreme youth. The investigation is said to have put the Government on the track of a more formidable conspiracy, with ramifications in Russian Poland, with a view to a general rising of all the Slavonic populations of Austria to form a republic, which would comprise some 9,000,000 of inhabitants.

DENMARK. A private letter of the 11th from Copenhagen speaks more hopefully of the probability of an amicable and early settlement of the differences between Denmark and the Frankfort Diet. In the last Council of Ministers, presided over by the King, it was decided that those paragraphs of the Constitution which have not been submitted to discussion in the Estates of Holstein shall be abrogated, as well as the decrees of the 23rd of June, 18/56, concerning the determination of the special or common affairs of the Duchies.

The plan of formation of the Federal Contingent has just appeared. It will be composed of troops of all arms ; 4,200 men for the principal contingent, a reserve of 1,200 more, and 600 of a supplementary contingent. Several of our large ships of war are to be fitted with screws. The great naval dock will soon be finished and inaugurated. The statue of King Frederick VI. has just been placed on its pedestal opposite the entrance of the Garden of Fredericksborg. M von Sclieele has lately arrived here. The King, of whom he had an audience, invited him to dinner at Skodsborg. The harvest in Denmark and the Duchies is expected to prove very superior to that of last year ; indeed, above an average. This, at least, was the opinion before the icceut storm, which has caused some damage, but not, it is thought, to a serious extent. According to the accounts from the Sound, the Two Belts, and the Cattegat, 20 vessels were lost during that terrible tempest.

(I'rnm the Weekly Despair, h, August 22 ) TURKEY. A strange affair has occurred at Constantinople : -A resident physician, Dr. Zalloni, an Austrian, was called in to prescribe for the favourite wife of a great Turkish personage, and on questioning her in the harem, he found that she was suffering from an inflammation of the bowels. He slightly touched with his finger the part affected ; on which a eunuch, who was in attendance, misinterpreting the act, rush I ed on him, knocked him down and heat hitn until he was half dead. The woman's husband hearing the noise, hurried in, and being told what hid taken place, stabbed the physician in the thigh with a dagger. The blow was so violent that the weapon broke. The wounded physician, bathed in blood, was removed to the

street and left to get home as well as lie could. l)r. Zalloni, a few days after, died of the injuries which he had received. The Constantinople correspondent of the Times says : þÿ The Sultan's expenditure has increased , is increasing, and ought to be cut down." Such is the universal cry which resounds through the whole Empire. The Minister, who is at the end of his wits and financial 1 gcrdennins, whispers it with a sigh; the employe, who gets paid in paper, murmurs it cautiously þÿ \ ears ; in arrear, raises it loudly ; the people, the army, which is months þÿ not to say who see the sweat of their brows squandered, utter it indignantly ; and even the usurer, who makes a fortune by this recklessness, afraid of the consequences, has begun to join in it clamorously. Never was the vox populi more clearly heard, and never was it more justly raised, llcforc it all mincing and delicacy would be out of place. It is high time to speak out plainly and expose the cancer which is consuming the vital f aces of this Empire. There is no secret about it, for it has become table-talk, and the evil has reached such a point, that, unle.-ssome remedy be found for it, the most serious consequences must follow. No Sovereign in Europe has a larger civil list than the Sultan of Turkey. According to the last arrangement, made about two years ago, it amounts to <£1,200,000 stlg., in round numbers, and surpasses by far that of any other Sovereign, if we compare it with the whole revenue of the empire, which is between

A"/, 000. 000 and 8,000,000 sterling. However formidable this proportion must appear to European minds, it might pass without comment in a country which might have the cheapest administration of any if it were strictly adhered to. 15ut iliis civil list represents only the nominal expenditure of the l'alace. In reality this latter knows no hounds except the impossibilit v of finding money. A considerable part of the revenues has been anticipated ; both the military and naval departments tire in arrcar ; in the army alone a sum of well-nigh a million of money is owing, the officials have been paid for the last two months in Treasury Bonds, which had to be discounted at 7 per cent, loss against paper money which was itself at a discount of (>0 to 70 per cent, against metallique. At the beginning of tins year two million's worth of thc-o Treasury Bonds had to he issued to pay the mo t crying debts of the civil list, and in ,-pito of all this the obligations of this department are estimated at more than twice that amount ; articles of the first necessity required for the Palace are left unpaid for months; most of the jewels have taken a pilgrimage, to one or another wearer, and are hawked about by the brokers. All these miseries, instead of producing a lucid interval, seem only to heighten the folly of extravagance. While one set of jewels is pawned, another richer is bought on credit from adventurous individuals. Two nuptials were celebrated this year for which the bill will not fall far short of <£700,000 to

£800,00 ) sterling, and two others are under consideration which will not cost much less. Besides, and far above all this, stands the building mania. If the thing were not patent it would he incredible, but at this moment not loss than eight palaces and live kiosks, and other smaller buildings, are in process of construction. These buildings, if they are now completed, will cost at least from £8,000,000 to £10,000,000 sterling. The thing has lately assumed such proportions that the Ministry, despairing to be able to do so, decided on making an attempt to check it The first step took place some weeks ago, when a memorandum, signed by all the Ministers, was given in, to ask tor a reduction of the pay of divers functionaries, and for the abolitiou of certain other posts which were unnecessary. It was represented that a great saving could be effected by the suppression of a number of useless officials, and that, consequently, more money could be made available for the purposes of Government. The representation was graciously received, and au answer promised. A few days after, the Ministry of Finance was called, and informed that his Majesty had a running account with his French fournissenr, who had furnished the new palace and was now finishing the theatre. This account was 150,000 purses or about £500,000, of which one-third was to he paid now, and that it was hoped the faithful Minister would provide the necessary sum. The next day a loan of 00,000,000 piastres was hawked about Galata, and part of the sum

T o c ft o i x a y i s found. When this was settled the memorandum about the retrenchment to he made was signed, Convinced, then, that beating about the bush would lead to nothing, a new representation, signed by all the Ministers, was given in, giving a picture of the deplorable financial condition of the country, and the impossibility to go on any longer at this rate. What the effect of it will be remains to be seen. Advices arc said to have been received in Paris from Trebizond of outrages having occurred in that quarter, arising from Mahometan fanaticism. Some eighty Turks made a razzia on a town called Santa, whilst the Christian inhabitants were at a church at some distance, which was surrounded, so as to prevent information reaching them. They then completely stripped the town, and outraged the women and girls. Persons who are in the daily habit of watching the different phases of Spanish policy will recollect that in the year 1820, after the fall of General Espartero, his successor, General I VDonnell, determined to organise an expedition for the chastisement of the Riff pirates, an expedition which would have been applauded by all parties, and especially by the army, which thirsts for occupation. NAPLES The correspondent of the Times writes on the 17th : þÿ "A portion of the foreign Press has lately fallen into gross error in regard to many incidents connected with Naples. One of the most recent statements of this kind is that which is published on the authority of the Paris correspondent of the Indepcndanrt llclge, that Setteinbrini, in accordance with his own request, h;is been permitted to go into perpetual exile. Nothing of the kind. Poor Set- , .nbrini i- st .1 confined in the island of St. Stefano ; aud his wile, who went to Genoa during the summer to see her son. has not been permitted to return Madame Poggi, the unfortunate mother of one of the Salerno prisoners condemned to 25 years in irons in the Island of Favignana, has just been ordered out ol the kingdom. She is to leave in eight days. The poor woman is in despair at leaving a country in which her only son is confined. No motive was given for the- command. nary precautions taken by the police, 1 may instance the following case : þÿ As the King was driving the other day, a man held up his hand with a petition. Montenegro. The Journal tie Constantinople of the 10th published a note which contains the following : " The Montenegrins, in contempt of the most solemn promises, have broken for the third time a truce agreed upon, aud, encouraged by the impunity they enjoy, have again penetrated with fire and sword into the Ottoman territory. On the 28th of July, they entered the small town of Kalachim, which contained no troops and was unprovided with any means of defence, and, falling like savage beasts on the unfortunate inhabitants, pitilessly massacred them ; after setting fire to their houses, they then retired, loaded with spoil. Neither age nor infancy was spared by those bandits. All the women who escaped the first massacre were carried off ; the handsomest were retained as booty, and the others murdered in cold blood." The note concludes with a hope that Europe will not be slow in branding with reprobation such acts of barbarism

Ilis white body, gleaming under the clear moonlight, could have been easily distinguished at a far greater distance. I had expected to see him much further away ; but, after all, the tilt of lances, and the menace delivered to the pursuing horsemen, had scarcely occupied a score of seconds, and ho could not in the time have gone out of sight. He was still running between myself and the foot of the hill þÿ apparently keeping along the bank of the stream. I put the Indian horse to his full speed. The point of my knife served for whip and spur. I was no longer encumbered with the spear ; it had been left in the body of Hissoo-royo. I kept my eyes fixed upon the steed, but ho was fast closing in to the timber that skirted the base of the hill ; he was nearing the bend where I had taken to the water, and would soou be hidden from my view behind the bushes. All at once I saw him swerve, and strike away to the left, across the open plain. To my surprise I saw this, for I had conjectured that his rider was aiming to reach the cover offered by the thicket. Without waiting to think of an explanation, I headed the mustang into the diagonal line, and galloped forward 1 was in hopes of getting nearer by the advantage thus given me, but I was ill satisfied with the creeping pace of the Indian horse, so unlike the long, free stretch of my noble Moro. Where

was he ? Why was I not bestriding him ? The white steed soon shot clear of the hill, and was now running upon the plain that stretched beyond it. I saw that I was not gaining upon him ; on the contrary, he was every moment widening the distance between us. Whore was Moro ? Why had he been taken away ? At that instant 1 perceived a dark hurst man making along the foot of the ridge, as if to intercept me ; he was dashing furiously through the thicket that skirted the base of the declivity. I could hear the bushes rattling against the flanks of his horse ; ho was evidently making all the haste in his power, at the same time aiming to keep concealed from the view of any one upon the plain. I recognised my horse, and upon his back the thin, lank form of the earless trapper ! We met the moment after, at the point where the thicket ended. Without a word passing between us, both simultaneously flung ourselves to the ground, exchanged horses, and remounted. Thank Heaven ! Moro was at last between my knees ! parted from him, ' gallip like darnation, an kitch 'Now, young fellur!' cried the trapper, as I up wi' her! We'll soon be arter on yur trail þÿ all right thur. Away !' I needed no prompting from Rube ; his speech was not finished before I had sprung my horse forward, and was going like the wind. It was only then that I could comprehend why the horses had been changed ; a ruse it was þÿ an after-thought of the cunning trappers ! Had I the Indians would in all probability have camp, mounted my own conspicuous steed by the sus-

pected something, and continued the pursuit ; it was the spotted mustang that had enabled me to carry out the counterfeit ! I had now beneath mo a horse I could depend upon ; and with renewed vigour I bent myself to the chase. For the third time, the black and þÿ white stallions were to make trial of their for the third time was it to bo a struggle speed between these noblo creatures. Would the struggle be hard, and long? Would flections as I swept onward in the pursuit. iny Moro again be defeated ? T -. « o x « . . & i. y i s the moon shining brightly, and the snow-white form, like a meteor, beaconed me onward. I had not galloped far, before perceiving that 1 rapidly gained upon the steed. Surely he was not running at his fleetest? Surely he was going more slowly than was his wont ? Oh ! could his rider but know who was coming after ! þÿ could she but hear me ! I would have called, but the distance was still too great. She could not have heard even my shouts ; how could she distinguish my voice ? I galloped on in silence. I was gaining þÿ constantly and rapidly gaining. Surely 1 was drawing nearer r or were my eyes playing false under the light of the moon 1 þÿ and slowly I fancied that the steed was heavily þÿ as if he was labouring in running heavily the race. I fancied þÿ no, it was no fancy þÿ I was sure of it ! Beyond a doubt, he was not going at his swiftest speed ! What could it mean ? Was he broken by fatigue ? Still nearer and nearer I came, until scarcely three hundred yards appeared between us. I fancied that my shouts might be heard, that my voice I called aloud ; I called the name of my betrothed, coupling it with my own ; but no answer came þÿ no sign of recognition to cheer me. I he ground that now lay between us favoured a race-course speed ; and I was about putting my horse to his full stretch, when, to my astonishment, I saw the steed stagger forward, and fall headlong to the earth ! It did not check my career, and in a few seconds more I was upon the spot, and halting over horse and rider, still prostrate.

I flung myself from the saddle, and drew nearer. Isolina had disengaged herself, and risen to her f'e, t. With her right hand clasping the red knife, she stood confronting me. ' Savage ! approach me not !' she cried in the Comanche tongue, and with a gesture that told her dcteimination. ' Isolina ! I ant not It is' ' Henri !' No words interrupted that wild embrace ; no sound could be heard save that made by our hearts, as they throbbed closely together. Silently I stood upon the plai ? with my betrothed in my arms. Moro was by our side, proudly curving his neck and chafing the steed between bis foaming lips. At our feet lay tbc prairic-horsc with tiie barb in bis vitals, and the feathered shaft protruding from bis side. His eyes were fixed and glassy ; blood still ran from bis spread nostrils ; but bis beautiful limbs were motionless in death ! Horsemen were seen approaching the spot. We did not attempt to flee from thctn : 1 recognised my followers. We looked back over the plain ; there was no sign of pursuit ; but for all that, we did not tarry there. We knew not bow soon the Indians might be after us ; the friends of Hissoo-royo might start forth upon the trail of Wakono ! It wa near daybreak when we halted to rest, and then only alter the prairie had been fired behind us. Wo found shelter in a pretty grove of acacias, and a grassy turf on which to repose. My wearied followers soon fell asleep. 1 slept not ; 1 watched over the slumbers of my betrothed. Her beautiful head rested upon

my knees ; her soft damask check was pillowed upon the robe of jaguar-skins, and my eyes were upon it. The thick tresses had fallen aside, and 1 saw The matador, too, had been merciful ! or had gold bribed him from bis cruel intent ? No matter which ! he had failed in his fiendish duty. 1 hero in full entirety were those delicate organs þÿ perfect, complete, I saw but the trifling scar where the gold circlet had been rudely plucked the source of that red hemorrhage that had been seen by Cyprio ! I was too bappy to sleep. It was our last night upon the prairies. Before the setting ot another sun, we bad crossed the Rio Grande, and arrived in the camp of our army. Under the broad protecting wings of the American eagle, my betrothed could repose in safety untill that blissfnll hour when

Of the Comanches we never heard more. The story of one only was afterwards told þÿ a fearful tale. Ill fated Wakono ! A horrid end was his. An oft-told tale by the prairie camp-fire is that of the skeleton of an Indian warrior found clasping the trunk of a tree ! Wakono had horribly perished. We had no design of giving liirn to such a fate. Without thought had we acted ; and though lie may have deserved death, we had not designed for him such terrible retribution. Perhaps I was the only one who had any remorseful feeling ; but the remembrance of that scalp-bedecked shield þÿ the scenes in that Cyprian grove þÿ those weeping captives, wedded to a wof'ul lot þÿ the remembrance of these cruel realities evermore rose before my mind, stifling the remorse 1 should otherwise have felt for the doom of the ill-starred savage. His death, though terrible in kind, was merited by his deeds, and was perhaps as just as punishments usually are. Poetical justice demands the death of Ijurrn, and by the hand of Holingsworth. Truth enables me to satisfy the demand. On my return to the camp, I learned that the act was already consummated þÿ the brother's blood bad been avenged ! It was a tragic tale, and would take many chapters in the telling. I may not give theui here. Let a few particulars suffice. Iroin that dread night, Ilolingswortb bad found a willirg band to aid him in his purpose of retribution þÿ one who yearned lor vengeance keenly as himself. Wheatley was the man. The two, with a chosen party, had thrown

themselves on the trail of the guerrilla, and with l'cdro as their guide, had followed it far within the hostile lines. Like sleuth-hounds had they followed it night and day, until they succeeded in tracking the guerrilleros to their lair. It was a desperate conflict þÿ baud to hand and knife to knife þÿ but the rangers at length triumphed ; most of the guerrilleros were slain, and the band nearly annihilated. Ijurra fell by Ilolingsworth's own hand ; while the death of the red ruffian El Zorro, by the bowic knife of the Texan lieutenant, was an appropriate punishment for the cruelty inflicted upon Conchisa. The revenge of hntli was complete, though both still bore the sorrow within their hearts. The expedition of the two lieutenants was productive of other fruits. In the head-quarters of the guerrilla they found many prisoners, Yankees and Ayankicudos þÿ among others, that rare diplomatist Don Ramon dc Vargas. Of course the old gentleman was released from captivity, and had arrived at the American camp, just in time to welcome his fair daughter and future son-in-law from their grand ««/e-hymencal 'tour upon the prairies.' the end of the war trail.

It is the tv suit of that steady advance of science ami civilization which is the marked characteristic of the nineteenth century . Ten yea's ago, no one could have dreamt of the wonderful applications of that mysterious po v. er of which man got the first idea Iron the convulsive motions of the limbs ot a dead frog. Now that the cable connecting the two hemispheres of the world is laid, we trust that our enterprising countryman, Captain Raasloff, will not be slow in bringing to our shores the blessings of this giant enterprise of the human mind ; than which, no stronger bond could ever be used to bind the nations of the world into one harmonious whole. We expect to learn further particulars of this interesting event by the British Mail Packet due at St. Thomas to-morrow.

The Atlantic Telegraph. þÿ There is good reason to hope that the great enterprise of uniting the Old and new Worlds, has at length proved successful ; that man's genius, industry and eneigv, have triumphed over time, distance, and the deep. We will not detract from the gratification which this news will occasion throughout the couutry, by any expression of doubt as to the success of the undertaking. Let us hope that it may be as complete as its most sanguine friends could wish, and that the 4th oi August, 1858, may be marked in the world's history, as the day on which the Oeeau Telegraph was successfully laid. ."should such prove to be the fact, we shall be able, at a distance of thousands of miles, to give and receive communications quicker than the light The geographical position of New York will enable us to obtain intelligence of events in Europe, several liours before tliey occur ! Being four hours in solar time West of the nearest European point þÿ i.e., four hours elapsing after mid-clay in Ireland, before midday in New York, þÿ we are placed in that seemingly paradoxical, but in reality true and auspicious position. Hence when the Telegraph is in full operation, we shall, ere noon, receive intelligence of the closing of the London Exchange at four o'clock in the afternoon of the same day. Arrangements will doubtless be made for transmitting intelligence with equal promptness from the different capitals and various important cities of the old world. i ii America is especially due the glory of this

invention Professor Morse may indeed have received a fortuitous hint, in that memorable passage which he made across the Atlantic nearly twenty years ag i ; but lie unquestionably amplified and improved upon it, with all the inductive power and inherent calculation of Frinklin, when, standing serenely and cbn- " lently upon earth, lie calmly, by the simple iu.-tiumentality of a kite and string, brought down the lightning from the height where the I bunder rolled. The experiment of the great diilosopher was comparatively unproductive; I. nt tli at of his modern successor has been eminent v practical, and, having been first applied tn nite Baltimore with Washington, lias progressively advanced until it joins two worlds together In a commercial point of view, the effect of the Ocean Telegraph will bo very important. It may. iudccd, put an end to those great speculations which have, until lately, been so hugely cmriod on, on both sides of the Atlantic, when twelve for more) days on an average separated its shores from each other : but it will promote a more healthy trade. The merchant will securely give, his orders, þÿ the stock- In nkcr ami the banker will issue his commands, þÿ with the certainty that neither can be materially affected by the condition of markets distant in point of position, though no longer of pace. We may thus no longer have so many of those colossal strokes by means of which (ortuues were realized at a blow, but wo shall be free from many of those individual reverses

which have hitherto followed the arrival of almost every steamer. In a moral point of view, the advantages will be great. It will no longer be in the power of the most rampant demagogue, or expatriated patriot, to sever nations which are thus closely united. All the ties of a common language, a general affinity, and for the most part of a similarity in institutions, will receive their last and most enduring touch from this electric wire ; and it is safe to predict that in future it will be almost impossible to involve the two untiuns in strife, when hostilities can

The Agamemnon after experiencing many n. ap and some stormy weather arrived on the 5th August at Valentia, the day after tlie arrival of the Niagara at Trinity Bay. Soon after her arrival a signal was received from the Niagara that they were preparing to land, having paid out 1,030 nautical miles of cable, while the Agamemnon had accomplished her portion of the distance with an expenditure of 1,020 miles, making the total length of the wire submerged 2,050 geographical miles. The following mes-age was received on Friday August 13, at the office of the Atlantic Telegraph tic Telegraph : þÿ Company, from Valentia, þÿ The receipt of a message of 26 by British and Irish Magnewords yesterday evening from Newfoundland, relative to signals and instruments, has satisfied me as to the cause of delay in the full and free interchange of messages. We can receive at very good speed from them, while they can as yet only receive from us slowly. 1 hope to be able to transmit the message Irom her Majesty to the President this þÿafternoon. The Cherbourg fetes commenced on the 3rd August. Queen Victoria and the Prince Consort arrived the day after, and were entertained at dinner by the Emperor of the French, on board the line-of-battle ship La Bretagne. The Emperor, in proposing the toast of the health of her Majesty and ol the Royal Family of England, made a speech, in which he said" I am happy to be

enabled to express the sentiments by which 1 am animated upon this occasion of the þÿQueen v s isit to Cherbourg. The facts do indeed speak for themselves, and prove that the hostile passions which were excited by some unfortunate incidents have never been able to alter either the friendship which exists between the two Crowns, or the desire of the people to remain at peace. I have, therefore, the firm hope that if any attempts were made to revive again the rancours of a former period, such attempts would be foiled by the good sense of the public, as the waves are baffled by yonder breakwater, which at this moment serves to protect the squadrons of both empires against the violence of the þÿsea. The Prince Consort, on behalf of her Majesty, responded to the toast, m doing which he said, þÿ The Queen is most sensible of the words we hayejust heard, which will for ever be dear to her. TheQueen is doubly happy in having an opportunity, by her presence here, to join the Emperor in endeavouring to draw together as closely as possible the ties of friendship which exist between the two nations. The friendship has their mutual prosperity for its basis, and the blessing of Heaven will not be wanting to confirm þÿit. The Emperor attaches so much importance to the visit 'of Queen Victoria to Cherbourg, that he has commanded a pyramid of granite to be erected at the head of the new dock to perpetuate the remembrance of that remarkable event. It is said also that a marble slab is being cut in Paris, to be placed in the Maritime

Prefecture at Cherbourg, to record the invitation the Queen of England accepted and her visit to that place. UNITED STATES. Tlie movements of the Mormons at Utah appear as indecisive and uncertain as ever. On the 3rd of July they had all returned to the city and their homes in the different parts of the territory. General Johnston had passed through the city with his horses, and encamped thirty miles on the other side of it. No troops were in the city. The Government officers had been duly installed in their various offices, and were prepared for the proper discharge of their duties. Brigham Young was anxious to be tried on the charge of treason, but insisted that the jury should consist of Mormons only ! A letter from New York alleges that þÿ Geneþÿral Walker has just come out with some disclosures which, if true, are certainly damaging to the Administration. He alleges, in a letter to a Mobile paper, in reply to an article appearing in the Washington Union, the official organ, that whilst Floyd, the Secretary at War, assured General Ilenningsen, þÿWalker right- s hand man, that the Government would feel bound to resist any filibustering attempt on Nicaragua, he advised Walker strongly to enter the service of Mexico, and, whilst in that position, either by hauling down tlio Spanish flag, or some other such device, to involve Spain in a quarrel with Mexico, so that the United States might have an opportunity of seizing on Cuba.

BRITISH COLUMBIA. The American papers are filled with every variety of laet and speculation in reference to the Fraser River gold discoveries. A private letter to the New York Herald says: þÿ þÿ The discovery of gold on Fraser River, and its effect on California, constitute an epoch in our history. The new mines threaten to take off one-fourth of our male population. The excitement is very great. Nothing is thought of but the new þÿmines. In the same vein, one of the San Francisco exchanges, after crying down this new gold citement as an immense humbug, says þÿ Down exthe Sacramento, night after night, pours a torrent of emigration for the new El Dorado. Every steamer from the interior reaches San Francisco loaded to the every town and guards mining with a camp living freight. they come þÿ þÿ hardy From sons of þÿtoil þÿ daring þÿ þÿadventurers þÿ þÿ the bone and sinew of the þÿState.' þÿ Our streets are crowded with them, our hotels swarm with them, and our wharves almost groan beneath their weight þÿ þÿtide. The fever rages with more than usual It is useless to attempt to stem the virulence, and those who have become infected with it will hear nothing, listen to nothing, think of nothing, dream of nothing, but Fraser River and its golden þÿsands. þÿ is It possible that, if the news from the British possessions should continue favourable, twenty-five per cent of our whole mining population will proceed there. þÿ In British Columbia itself arrangements have been made to meet the emergency. No vessels

or canoes are allowed to go up the river, nor any passenger without a licence. The Satellite, guards its mouth. No spirituous liquuis are permitted to be taken up to be sold to the Indians ; no articles for trade arc allowed, nothing but a six þÿmonths supply for the miners themselves. Governor Douglas and Captain Provost, of the Satellite, have appointed custom-house officers and chosen magistrates from the diggers themselves. All who trade with the Indians or who sell them spirituous liquors are to have their property confiscated ; and i i two instances this regulation has been carried out. Rome account of the natural features of the district is given by a San Francisco paper : þÿ þÿ Fraser River undergoes two falls each year, the first occurring in .Tune and the second in August. The freshet between June and August is caused by the melting of the snow in the Rocky Mountains, and pouring down through Thompson River The Indians are quite peaceable, hut exceedingly troublesome. As soon as a miner lays down his pick an Indian stands by to make use of it for himself, and when he lays down his shovel for the pick the Indian takes the shovel. They are all engaged in mining þÿ even to children four and five years of age, and are as well posted on the value of gold as the whites. Mr Ettling saw one Indian who had 200 dollars in a buckskin purse, dug out by himself in one week. Wild ducks and geese are plentiful at the mouth of the river, but no game had been seen beyond
that point. Salmon, however, was abundant, an<l easily taken. The natives represent the winters as being excessively bitter and þÿcold.

Mr. Bright is now making arrangements for landing the end and thus bringing to a successful termination his anxious and dilficult task. From the time the Agamemnon left Queenstown, on the j 18th of July, until she joined the rest of the squadron at the rendezvous in mid ocean on the 29th, she experienced a continued succession of heavy winds. The splice was successfully made on the started noon of the 29th, and the ships aftertowards their several stations. The whole distance from Trinity Bay, Newfoundland, to Valentia is about 1,650 nautical lines, and this has been covered by 2,022 miles of cable. The slack, therefore, is just 372 miles, or about 22£ per cent.

In our last Number wc bad tlie gratification of recording the well-earned triumph won by perseverance and skill in the completion of the Atlantic Telegraph. This achievement of science and energy was completed on Thursday week, iu spite of unfavourable weather, the two ships reaching their respective destinations nearly at the same time ; and, as soon as the machinery in Newfoundland is complete, a conversation may be carried on between Europe and America, nearly as fast as across a dinner table Articulate messages have already passed along the bottom of the Atlantic, by a chord as sensitive as the nerves along which commands and impressions run between our bodily organs and the brain. A very interesting account þÿ too long, we regret, for our columns þÿ has been given in the daily papers of the successful voyage of the Agamemnon in laying the Atlautic cable. At one time a whale crossed the line, just grazing it ; twice vessels bore down upon them, threatening destruction; and several times anxiety was created by the failure of the continuity signals, or apparent damages in the cable, and it was with excited feelings the shore was reached in safety. Mr. Mansfield, surgeon, U.N., who accompanied the expedition, gives the subjoined acmemnon s share in laying the cable : þÿ count, dated Valentia, August 6, of the Aga- þÿ Her þÿMajesty s ships Gorgon and Valorous left Queenstown in the early part of Saturday, July 17. We ( Valorous) reached the rendezvous, lat. 52 þÿ5 N., long 32 þÿ42 W., on the

24th. The Niagara, the Gorgon, and the j Agamemnon arrived on the 25th, 2Gth, and 28th respectively, the Niagara having sailed from Cork harbour on the evening of the same day that we left, the Agamemnon at 3 a.m. on the 18th. Our boats having conveyed the end of the cable from the Niagara to the Agamemnon early on the 29th, it was spliced and lowered i into the þÿ depths of the þÿoceau at 1.5 (observ. 1 time), the ships steaming apart at 1 25 p.m. It was found on board the Agamemnon that it was necessary to stop at 8 30 p.m., in order to diminish ns much as possible the tension on a weak portion of the cable, which was allowed pier find run been j to easily out in safety. An announcement made to the effect that, should the carrying it, out from both the Niagara and the Agamemnon, cable part before 15.) nautical miles had run we were all to return to rendezvous, and an intense anxiety was accordingly felt as the critical time was approaching. That, however, was passed, to the comfort of all, when, at 2.15 p.m. on the 30th, the Agamemnon signalled that her allotted portion had been paid out in safety þÿ a similar result being obtained at 3.30 p.m. iu the Niagara. Hitherto nothing could been more gratifying than the calm state of the sea and weather, and all were sanguine of success to a high degree, when towards cvcninir on the 30th the wind commenced to freshen, and before midnight it blew half a gale from S.S E., a heavy swell getting up and causing a violent pitching motiou to the ship

Great fears were entertained for the safety > the cable all night, but in the morning it was still secirc, having withstood a heavy continued until the 3rd of August, when it commenced to diminish and to be less felt, as the wind shifted to S.W. on the day before, and was now favourable We from the deep into the shoal water þÿ i.e., from 1775 fathoms of soundings into 550 fa thorns, at seven p.m. on the 3rd inRt. in lat. 52 þÿ27 N., long. 16 þÿ7 W., and at noon yesterday (Wednesday), the 4th, we were in 415 fathoms.

86Y miles distant from Vnlentia Last night, at nine p. in., being less than forty miles off, we left the Agamemnon , proceeding so as to make the land before her in the morning; we made it soon and anchored after daylight, the Agamemnon coining up at six this morning. We anchored in Donlus Bay, outside Valentin harbour, and the cable was landed by our boats, under the command of Lieutenant Richmond Moore (senior Lieutenant of her þÿMajesty ship s Valorous), at White Strand Bay, off Donlus Bay, in the forenoon, amidst the greetings and welcomes of all who were assembled to receive j it. There were not, however, very many present, ns our arrival could not, of course, have been anticipated. Thus the end of an unparalleled undertaking has at last been attained, after many a combat with storm and sea, and hard struggling against apparently insurmountable difficulties. However, this satisfactory result well repays the greatest expenditure of j energy in its achievement. The cable has been laid down at the season recommended by' Lieutenant Maurcy, LL.D., though the weather at the end of June, when the last attempts were made, was decidedly the most favourable, and it evidently would have succeeded had there not been mechanical defects in the cable itself. has been about 30. The two great facts were simultaneously made known ; the one amid the blaze and thunder of three thousand guns, the other by an unexpected paragraph in the newspapers. Lint, compared with the one fact, how j federal union under the British Crown, and paltry is the other ! The submersion of the Atlantic wire robs of most of its importance the demonstration of Cherbourg. When the Emperor of the French proposed the health of | feel to lie essential to their pi osperity and good Queen Victoria on his own soil, in his own harbour, and spoke of that peace which is alike his interest and bis duty, it was well. The noblest work of our age and race was accomplished, and the war-gods of Europe

were reminded that þÿl eacc had its victories more stupendous than Battle ever wrought or 1 than ail Ambition ever dreamt of. Let the Queen and the Emperor shake hands, for good may re- , of them. There have been coni i : i .ns sult ; but, when America and Great Britain talk to each other under the waters of the Atlantic, good is certain, and evil all but impossible. The other scientific marvels of modern times, from' the invention of the Printing-press and the discovery of America, down to the full adaptation of the Steam-Engine and the Rail- \ those of common way to the purposes of locomotion, have not as yet produced the fruits expected of them. Notwithstanding the diffusion of knowledge by7 | ideas. means of the printing-press, and the increased intercourse due to steam locomotion, the populations of Europe and Asia are but imperfectly acquainted with each other. Differences of language, of manners, of habits, and of religious faith keep them and apart, and will long continue to do so. They will doubtless share to some extont the advantages of telegraphic communication between the Old World and the New ; but the main benefits will fall to the lot of Great Britaiu and America. These nations are almost the sole depositaries of human freedom. They represent the liberty, the intelligence, and the enterprise of our time. Closely united by blood, language, and education, they will become united still more closely by interest and friendship, now that they can commu-

nicate their thoughts, wants, and wishes by means of electricity. Between them will be formed an alliance the most natural and the most beneficial possible in the present confused and imperfect relations of humanity ; and the probability of war will be as far removed into the future as the probability of hostile collision I squabbles of Europe

between our globe and any wandering comet of which astronomers may have cognisance. But if such are likely to be the international results, whilst not one or two wires, but twenty, are throbbing under the waves of the ocean with the messages of trade, diplomacy, and affection, what are to be the results to the British Empire itself? a «#m CHRISTIANSTED, ST. CROIX TUESDAY, 7tii SEPTEMBER, 1858. Onl of t!v lost remarkable characteristics of the present age is the rapidity by which improvement follows on discovery. As late as is the application of Galvanism to the transmission ot messages, improvement lollows on in provement, until a high degree of perfection has already been attained. From the system of Morse, by which letters are expressed by particular combinations of lines and dots, advancement was made to the printing telegraphs of House and Brett; and, as if to prove that there is nothing perfect under the sun, we are informed by the London Timer, that a Chevalier Bonelli is now in Paris on business connected with the submarine ne between Sardinia and Algeria, and has b ought with him the apparatus of his ew invention, þÿ the autographic telprapi i> which a fursimile of writing s tra cin'. þÿ <1, the inscription on a slip of per, inserted re- on one extremity of the line, beii g exactly þÿ produced at the other. says the Times, of this system is obvi- þÿ One þÿadvantage a ous ; mistakes in transmission, now so frequent and inconvenient, are rendered impossible. As the message is written at one end, so it appears at the other. Another advantage is rapidity þÿ gain of time. It takes but four or five seconds to transmit a message of 25 words, which may be written on two or three lines. The shorter the slip of paper inserted between the rollers, the more rapid is the þÿtransmission. The same paper informs us that a conference of telegraph directors was to have

been held at Berne on the 25th August, for the purpose of introducing as much unity as possible of into the working of and lines, harmonizing systems, the various of consulting on various matters of interest, Belgium, France, Piedmont, Portugal, Spain, and Switzerland will there be represented. The Patrie devotes an article to the conduct of Hanover on the question ot the Duchies, and expresses surprise that the Government which, perhaps, of all others, is the one that has shown the least regard to the maintenance of its own constitutions, should prove the most ardent defender of the special constitution of Holstein against Denmark. It remarks that in 1837 King Ernest Augustus, on ascending the throne, abolished the constitution of 1833, and replaced it by the less liberal one of 1819. The Estates of the kingdom appealed to the German Diet, which declared itself inj competent, but which subsequently affirmed its competency when the Hano- UNDERSIGNED being about to ! verian nobility, supported bv King George, sought and effected important anti-liberal
in 1848. The respect of Hanover for the sanctity of constitutions is evidently of recent date, and is pretty generally attri-

, isting between the Hanoverian nobility and that of the Duchy of Holstein You are aware of the part recently played by Hanover with respect to the Danish proposals of the 15th of July, and of the tenacity with which her delegate protested against the favourable report drawn up by the committee with respect to those proposals. It can hardly be said that Denmark has shown undue stubbornness in the question. She proposes to suspend the constitution as regards Holstein and Luuenburg, and to enter into negotiations on the other matters in dispute. As regards some of these þÿ as, for instance, the abolition of the Ministry for the common constitution þÿ she has already done what was wished. She would have readily submitted the whole affair to arbitration; but to this the Confederation would not consent, maintaining the question to be a purely German one, in which no strangers should he allowed to meddle. The French Government has, I understand, in its diplomatic communications with the disputing parties, unilormly recommended a conciliatory course, and that they should, by mutual concessions, accomplish a settlement, and not allow the question to become a European one.
