THE WAR-TRAIL. A ROMANCE. BY CAPTAIN MAYNK REID. CHAPTER XO. TAKING TO Tilt WATER. I spent 'Ut little time in preparations; those had been made already It remained only to tighten my saddle-girt, look to tlie caps of my revolvers, and place both pistols and knife in the belt behind my hack ; there the weapons would be concealed by tlie pendent robe ot jaguarskins In a few minutes I was ready. I still loitered a while, to wait ior the falling of the water ; not long þÿ 1 was too anxious to nijrfi I might he too tarry þÿ long. The hour late of the council might bo for the crisis Not long did I loiter. It was not necessary. Even by tlie moonlight, we could distinguish the dark line of tlie bank separating the grassy turf current the water. Tlie rippling from t he surface of was shining like silver-lace, and, by contrast, the dark earthy strip that rose vertically above it, could he observed more distinctly. It was sensibly broader. 1 could wait no longer. 1 leaped into the saddle. My comrades crowded around me to say a parting word; with a wisii or a prayer upon tlioir lips, one after another pressed my hand. Some doubted of their over seeing me þÿagain l could tell this from tlie tone of their leave-taking; other were more confident. All vowed to revenge mo if I fell. Rube and Garey wont witli me down the hill. At the point where the stream impinged upon it, there were bushes ; these continued up the declivity, and joined the timber upon the summit Under their cover we had descended, reaching

the bank just at the salient angle of the bend. A thin skirting of similar bushes ran around the base of the hill, and following the path by which we had come, the ambuscade might have been moved a little nearer to the camp. But the cover was not so good as the grove upon the summit, and in case of a retreat, it would he necessary to gallop up the naked face of the slope, and thus expose our numbers. It was decided, therefore, to leave the men where they were. From the bend to the Indian camp, the river trended almost in a straight line, and its long reach lay before my eyes like a band of shining metal. Along its hanks, the bush extended no further. A single step towards tlie camp would havo exposed me to the view of its occupants At this point, therefore, it was necessary for me to take to the water; and dismounting, I made ready for the immersion, The trappers had spoken their last words of instruction and counsel ; they had both grasped my hand, giving it a significant squeeze that promised more than words ; but to these, too, had they given utterance.

þÿ þÿDon be t afeerd, þÿcapt n! said the younger. þÿ Rubeand I þÿwon be t far off. If we hear your pistols, þÿwe make ll a rush þÿto rst you, and meet you half-way any-how ; and if anything should happen þÿ þÿ you may depend þÿon þÿwe þÿamiss þÿ here Garey spoke with emphasis t lltake a bloody þÿrevenge. þÿ Yces! echoed Rube, þÿ we lldo jest thet. þÿThur be ll many a nick in Targuts afore next Krissmuss ef you ur rubbed out, young fellur ; thet I swar to ye. But þÿdon be t skeeart ! Keep yur eye sharp-skinned, an yur claws steady, an þÿthur no s fear but þÿyu ll git clur. Oncest yu clur þÿo the camp, þÿ ee may þÿreck o n n us. Bu straight for the timmer, an gallip as ef Ole j Scratch wur agruppiu at the tail þÿo yur þÿcritter. I waited to hear no more, but leading Moro down the bank, at the place where it sloped, 1 stepped gently into the current. My welltrained steed followed without hesitation, and in another instant we were both breast-deep in the flood. The water was just the depth 1 desired. There was a half yard of bank that rose vertically above the surface ; and this was sufficient to shelter either my own head, as I stood erect, or the frontlet of my horse. Should the channel continue of uniform depth as far as the camp, the approach would be easy indeed ; and, for certaiu hydrographic reasons, I was under the belief it would. The plumes of the Indian bonnet rose above the level of the meadow-turf, and as the leathers þÿ dyed of gay þÿcolours would have formed a conspicuous object. I took off the gaudy head-

dress, and carried it in my hand. I also raised the robe of jaguar-skin over my shoulders, in order to keep it dry ; and for the same reasoD, temporarily carried my pistols above the water-line. The making of these slight alterations occupied only a minute or so; and as soon as they were completed, I moved forward through the water. The very depth of the stream proved a circumstance in my favour. In wading, both horse and man make less noise in deep than in shallow water; and this was an important consideration. The night was still þÿ too still for my wishes þÿ and the plunging sound would have been heard afar off; but fortunately ihere were rapids below þÿ just where the stream forced its way through the spur of the hill þÿ and the hissing sough of these, louder the still night, in was borne upon the air to the distance of many miles. Their noise, to my own cars, almost drowned the plashing made by Moro and myself. I had noted this point d'avantoge before embarking upon the enterprise. At the distanco of two hundred yards from the bushes, 1 paused to look back. My purpose was to fix in my memory the direction of the hill, and more especially the point where my comrades had been left in ambush : in the event of a close pursuit, it would not do to mistake their exact situation. I easily made out the place, and saw that, for several reasons, a better could not have been chosen. The trees that timbered the crest of the hill were of a peculiar kind þÿ none more so upon the earth. They were a species of arbo-

rescent yucca, then unknown to botanists. Many of them were forty feet in height ; and their thick angular branches, and terminal fascicles of rigid leaves, outlined against Ihe sky, formed a singular, almost an unearthly spectacle. It was unlike any other vegetation upon earth, more resembling a grove of cast iron than a wood of exogenous trees. Why I regarded the spot as favourable for an ambush, was chiefly this: a party approaching it from the plain, and climbing the hill, might fancy a host of enemies in their front; for the trees themselves, with their heads of radiating blades, bore a striking resemblance to an array of plumed gigantic warriors. Many of the yuccas were only six feet in height, with tufted heads, and branchless trunks as gross as the body of a man, and they might readily have been mistaken for human beings. I saw at a glance the advantage of the position. Should the Indians pursue me, and 1 should succeed in reaching the timber before them, a volley from my comrades would check the pursuers, however numerous. The nine rifles would bo enough, with a few shots from the revolvers. The savages would fancy nine hundred under the mystifying shadows of that spectral-like grove

With confidence, strengthened by these considerations, I once moro turned my face upstream; and þÿ breasting the current, kept on. CHAPTER XC1. UP-STREAM. My advance was far from being rapid. The water was occasionally deeper or shallower, but generally rising above my liips þÿ deep enough to render wading a task of time and difficulty. The current was of course against me ; and though not very swift, seriously impeded my progress. I could have advanced more rapidly, but for the necessity of keeping my head and that of my horse below the escarpment of the bank. At times it was a close fit, with scarcely an inch to spare ; and in several places I was compelled to m with my neck bent, and my þÿhorse nose s h< Id down to the surface of the water. At intervals, I paused to rest myself þÿ for the exertion of wading against the current wearied me, and took away my breath. This was particularly the ease when I was required to crouch ; but I chose my resting-places where the channel was deepest, and where I could stand erect. I was all the while anxious to look up and take a survey of the camp : I wished to ascertain its distanco aud position ; but I dared not raise my head above the level of the bank. The sward that crowned it was smooth as a mown meadow, and the edge-line of the turf even and unbroken. Had 1 shewn but my hand above it, it might have been seen in that clear white light. I dared not shew either hand or head. 1 had advanced I knew not how far, but 1 fancied I must b o tr the lines. All the way,

I had kept close under the left bank, which, as Rube had predicted, now rose a lull half yard above the water line. This was a favourable circumstance, and another equally so was the fact that the moon on that þÿ the eastern side þÿ was yet low in the sky, and consequently the bank flung a broad black shadow that extended nearly half-way across the stream. In this shadow I walked, and its friendly darkness sheltered both myself aud my horse. I fancied I must be near the Hues, and longed to reconnoitre them, but, for the reasons alieady given, dared not. I was equally afraid to make any further advance þÿ for that might be still more perilous. 1 had already noted the direction of the wind : it blew from the river, aud towards the camp ; and should I bring my horse opposite the line of the mustangs, 1 would then be directly to windward of them, and in danger from their keen nostrils. They would be. almost certaiu to take up the scent of my steed, and utter their warning snorts. The breeze was light, but so much the worse. There was sufficient to carry the smell, and not enough to drown the plunging noise necessarily made by my horse moving through the water, with the hollow pounding of bis hoofs upon the rocks at the bottom. If I raised my head over the bank, there was the danger of being observed ; if I advanced, the prospect was one of still greater peril. For some moments I stood hesitating þÿ uncertain as to whether 1 should leave my horse, or lead him a little further. 1 heard noises from I This

the camp, but they were not distinct enough to guide me. I looked back down the river, with the hope of being able to calculate the distance I had come, and by that means decide where I was ; but my observation furnished no data by which I could determine iny position. With my eyes almost on a level with the surface of the water, I could not judge satisfactorily of distance. I turned my lace up-stream again, and scrutinised the parapet line of the bank. Just then I saw an object over its edge that answered well to guide me ; it was the croup and hip-bones of a horse þÿ one of the mustangs staked near the bank. I saw neither the head nor shoulders of the animal ; its hind quarters were towards the stream ; its head was to the grass þÿ it was browsing. The sight gratified me. The mustang was full two hundred yards above the point I had reached, I knew that its position marked the outer line of the encampment. 1 was just in the place where I wanted to be þÿ about two hundred yards from the lines. Just at that distance I desi d to leave my horse. I had taken the precaution to bring with me my picket-pin one of þÿ the essentials of the prairie traveller It was the work of a moment to delve it into the bank

I needed not to drive it with violence : my welltrained steed never broke fastening, however slight. With him the stake was only required as a sign that ho was not free to wander. In a moment, then, he was staked; aud with a þÿ þÿwhisper I parted from him, and kept on upstream. 1 had not gone a dozen yards further, when I perceived a break in the line of the bank. It was a little gully that led slantingly from the level of the prairie down to the bed of the stream. Its counterpart I perceived on the opposite side. The two indicated a ford or crossing used by buffaloes, wild-horses, and other_denizens of the prairie. At first, I viewed it with apprehension ; 1 feared it might uncover my body to the eyes of the enemy; but on coming opposite, my fears were allayed : t! slope was abrupt, and the high ground sereci d mo- as bwlore. Theie would be no danger in passing tin? place. As I was about moving o an idea arrested me ; aud I paused to regard the gully with a look of greater interest it offered me an advantage. I had been troubled about the position in which 1 had left my horse. Should I succeed in getting back, of course it would be under the pressure of a hot pursuit, and my steed was not conveniently placed; his back was below the level of the hank. He might easily be mounted, but how should I get out of the bed of the stream. Only by a desperate leap might he reach the plain above ; and he might fail in the effort. þÿ time might be lost, when time and speed would be most wanted.

I had been troubled with this thought ; it need trouble me no longer. The þÿ þÿcrossing afforded easy access either to or from the channel of the river þÿ the very thing 1 wanted. I was not slow to profit by the discovery. I turned back, aud having released the rein, led my horse gently up to the break. Choosing a spot undei the highest part of the bank, I fastened him as before, and there left him. I now moved with more ease and confidence, but with increased caution. I was getting too near to risk making the slightest noit-g, in the water ; a single plash might betray mo. It was my intention to keep in the channel, until I had passed the point where the hnrsi s were staked ; by so doing, I should avoid mossing the line of the horse-guards, and, what was quite as important, that of the horses themselves, for I was equally apprehensive of being discovered by the latter. Once inside their circle, they would take no notice of me, for doubtless theie would be other Indians within sight; and I trusted to my well-counterfeited semblance of savagery to deceive the eyes of the equine sentinels. I did not wish to go far beyond their lines; that would bring me in front of the camp itself þÿ too near its fires and its idle groups. I had noticed before starting thtjt there was a broad belt between the place occupied by the men, and that where their horses were staked. þÿ þÿneutral ground was little used by the camp loungers, and somewhere on the edg> of it I was desirous of making my entree.

I succeeded to my utmost wishes. Closely hugging the bank, I passed the browsing mustangs ; under their very noses I glided past, for I could hear them munching the herbage right over mo ; but so silently did 1 steal along, that neither snort nor hoof-stroke heralded my ad- | vancc. Iu a few minutes, I was sufficiently beyond them to make halt. I raised my head ; slowly and gently 1 raised it, till my eyes were above the level of the prairie slope. No one was near. I could sec the swarth savages grouped around their fires ; but they were a hundred yards off, or more. They were capering, and talking, and laughing ; but uo ear was bent, and co eye seemed turned towards me. No one was near I grasped the bank with my hands, and drew myself up. Slowly and sib ntly I ascended, liko some demon from the dark trap-door o stage On my knees, I reached the level of the turf , and, then gently rising to my feet, I stood crqct within the limits of the Indian campþÿ to all appearance as complete a savage as any upon the ground ! THE QUEEN AND THE CANADIANS. On Saturday evening Sir Edward Bulwer Lyttou, the Secretary of State for the Colonies, addressed an official communication to Mr. Norris, embodying the answer of Her Majesty to the petition, of which he was recently the bearer to this country, from citizens of Toronto and inhabitants of Canada. It will be recollected that the petition in question stated that a Crystal Palace similar in design, but of smaller dimensions to those of London and Paris, for the exhibition of the products of Canadian industry and skill, is in the course of erection in Toronto, and will be completed about the 1 st of October ; and the memorialists, remembering that Her Majesty had been pleased to honour the inauguration of similar undertakings in this country and elsewhere with her presence, prayed that she would confer a mark of favour on her loyal subjects in Canada, by giving authority to the Prince of Wales, or some other member of the Royal family, to proceed to Toronto and represent her at the opening of the Crystal Palace there. This doccment was signed by upwards of

s X\ & & o I a y i 180 of the chief citizens of Toronto and inhabitants of other parts of Canada, including, among others, Sir Alan M'Nab, the Hon. N. T. Belleau, the Speaker, and 25 members of the Legislature Council, the Hon. Henry Smith, Speaker of the Legislative Assembly, Mr. Brown, the recent Premier, Mr. Macdonald, the pre :nt head of the Government, and a large tv .nber of men of all parties in that bran ii of the Legislature ; Chancellor Blake md eight, other of the judges, both tl Protestan! and Roman Catholic Bishop Toronto, the Mayor and corporation of tin:' ty, the Mayor and town-council ot Hamilton, the President of the Board ot Trade, and several of the military authorities high in command. The idea of inviting a member of the Royal family to Canada, to grace the opening of the Crystal Palace, appears to have originated with Mr. Norris himself, a private citizen, but it speedily became so popular among the citizens that, although only some ten days were spent in putting it in execution, the most iuHuential of them endorsed and sanctioned it to the extent just described. It was then far on in August, the Crystal Palace was to be opened early in October, and it was evident that no time was to be lost in transmitting the view petition to this country if the object I ne was to have a chance ofsucce;-. in proper course in such cases is to transmit such a document through the Governor of Major Lang suspects that it is not now so , the colony, but Mr. Norris was unlearned

Sir Edmund Head, he brought the petition to England himself, instead of sending it through his Excellency's hands. This circumstance, it seems, has ratio r detracted from the character and effect of Mr. Norris's mission ; but still the memorial bore upon the face of it such strong evidence of the extent and spontaneity of the popular feeling in Canada on the subject to which it related that its promoters might perhaps be excused for overlooking some necessary formality, and the Colonial Secretary himself has so regarded it. Sir Bulwer Lytton, in the letter he has just addressed to Mr. Norris, is understood to have stated, after a passing reference to the departure from the ordinary custom, in not transmitting the petition through the deemed the province, that he had Governor of it his duty, considering the eminence of the persons whose names were attached to if, to lay it before the Queen, who had b u pleased to under she was receive it very graciously, though the necessity of declining the request that his Royal Highness the Prince of Wales or some other member of the Royal family should proceed to Canada with the view of opening the Crystal Palace at Toronto. Nor do I presume to think that I have devised the best i'orm and disposition for the vessel, it being enough for my purpose to show that the conception and execution of so formidable a machine is perfectly simple and practicable. CHRISTIANSTED, ST. CROIX FRIDAY, I5tii OCTOBER, 1858. There is at present a subject of great public inconvenience which wo think calls for official interference. We allude to the non-acceptance of five and ten stiver pieces on the part of shop keepers anil others. Wc have even been in- !

formed that they are refused at the Communal Treasury ; but we scarcely credit the report, since wc are aware, that they have not been i refusod at the Royal Treasury. It is easy to account for the semi-destruction of these coins. Every one is aware that our rural population delight in decorating their persons with small coins during their crop-over festivals, and for this purpose holes are punc- | turn! in every one which they possess. We have even heard of their using thrce-dollar-bills as breast plates. This partial destruction of our coins can only be prevented by calling in those that are punctured and making the act punishable afterwards. Meanwhile some steps should he taken to restore confidence in the value of those now in circulation.

Frnm thc'Xnc Yuri: Timex , September 21. LATEST FROM AMERICA. The Atlantic Cable Reported All Right. Trinity Bay, N F., Thursday, Sept. 2.'!. Wc can at last announce the gratifying intelligence that the Atlantic Cable is again in complete working order. Good electrical currents have been passed through the line for the last three days, and though wc are not informed of the transmission of any specific messages, it can he stated with accuracy that the þÿ þÿsignals þÿreceived from Valentia areas perfect as ever. It is hoped the cable will be ready for business in a few weeks at the furthest.

The Caiilk not Broken, and hie Continuity Perfect. þÿ The despatch which we publish this morning states that the cable is not only not broken, hut that the signals received from Valentia at Trinity Bay are as perfect as ever. Wc never had any doubts of the complete success of the enterprise ; and all bough we have not received a message over the line since the 1st inst., we knew, as we have frequently stated, that as soon as better instillments than those which were first used could be put upon the line, the result would satisfy the most sanguine. þÿ Good electrical currents have been passing through the line for the last three þÿdays; hut why, it may he justly asked, have we not been informed of this before ? The only answer to this question is to he found in the unwillingness of the English electricians, who have now charge of the terminus at Trinity- Bay, and who have persistently declined to satisfy the American public with any information, although repeatedly asked. These gentlemen are evidently dissatisfied with the action of the company in dismissing the chief electrician, Dr. Whitehouse, whose instruments they have a particular interest in, and whose defective system they expected to see employed in the working of the cable, to

the exclusion ot" all others. Dr. \\ hitchouse, himself, in a letter to one of the London papers, states that there should he no fears for the safety of the line, and we may add, that as soon as Mr. þÿHughes instruments, which previous experiments have proved to ho the host, arc employed, we will .eceivo daily' despatches for publication from the other side. The only difficulty, let us again repeat, was in the employment imperfect of instruments, and owing to the dismissal of the chief electrician, which the company have evidently regarded as unavoidable, we have not and could not receive any communication till Mr. þÿHughes instruments supplied their place. The manner in which some of our daily papers explain the long interruption which has taken place in the transmission of messages is ludicrous to those who arc at all conversant with the subject. Are they aware that the cables which have been laid across the Mediterranean þÿ a sea which is remarkable for the volcanic character of its bottom, and for the abrupt and þÿ is m irked are still more perfect, so far as their precipitous declivities by which it electrical condition is concerned, than when they' were submerged. But they had doubts bout the existence of the great oceanic plae au, although they have had none, it seems, in regard to the mountain peaks from which they say the cable is suspended. þÿYes and these same wiseacres were confident that the cable woul 1 not be laid ; but the accomplishment of the. work showed what fools tin y' had

made of themselves, ns the transmission of messages in the course of a few days more will prove how stupid they have been in insisting that the cable is broken. The best thing which the 1'lnglish directors can do is to place the further management of the enterprise in the hands of Mr. Field, withit, whom they would never have laid the le ; for the. bungling manner in which they I , acted shows that they cannot get along if left to themselves. Mr. Field should not have resigned his office as general manager, at estab- until a regular daily communication was least lished between the two worlds. The refusal of the el ctricians at Trinity Bay to give any information regarding the. cable may be traced to this resignation, for there is no denying the fact that tin y- have all along adhered to Dr. Whitehouse, and done all in their power to throw obstacles in the way of þÿl rof. Hughes. Their indifference to the feelings of the American public is highly reprehensible, and wo trust the Hire dors will show their disapproval of it in a marked manner.

( DENMARK. j From the London Times' Correspondent.) Paris, Wednesday, Sept. 8, li p.m. Now that diplomatic Europe, weary of wordy contest, is enjoying rep þÿ that, nearly all pressing or perilous questions ; in satisfactorily disposed ol þÿ that secretaries and clerks in Foreignoffices and chancelleries are reduced, for want of occupation, to pen-mending, caricature-drawing, and newspaper-reading þÿ that foreign messengers unprofitable inaction þÿ have huug up their spurs and are vegetating in now, in sli , that, with the exception of the never-ending Turkish | troubles, Europe seems to have wound up all its ! foreign transactions and to be reduced to idlcj ness, of which it will soon be tin d, the moment | appears opportune to grant attention to .a question that, properly managed, might be pleasantly j settled, but which neglect might easily convert into a peril for the general tranquillity. 1 refer I to the long-standing difference between Denmark and the German Diet. This question of the Duchies has been pending a i intolerably long time, and the great Bowers < could not do better than to tender their good . in 1 r to facilitate its settlement for and all. Sparks neglected and suffered t inetiincs break out into dangerou- ere is not, it is to he hoped, much risk of th. dug to a dangerous pass between L nmari: at rmany ; hut, even admitting that, there is a;, it reason why the European Bowers, thci e s wholly uninterested in the matter, might wiili propriety proffer friendly a intervention. Den-

mark is a small and feeble country, although none will deny the valour and hardihood of her sons ; Germany, the Colossus, would make but a mouthful of her little Scandinavian neighbour; and, as is too apt happen disputes to in between the strong and the weak, there is sonic appearance of an overbearing disposition on the part of the big disputant. Ccrtaiu it is that his demands, ! moderate at first, have increased to unreasonable | dimensions. About two years ago Austria and Brussia asked the correction of certain vices of form in the þÿl rovincial Constitution of Holstein. Denmark, which appears to have acted all along in perfect good faith, could not but admit that there were grounds for the demand, þÿl ut subsequently the Diet went further ami further, until at last it put forward the pretension of 1 interfering not only with the Constitution of the German Duchies, hut also with that of the Danish Monarchy. Aud, unreasonable ns it may appear, it nevertheless is a fact that, while retiming, or at least neglecting compliance with the I reiterated request of the Danish Government tude 41 IS, created a deep sensation throughout ! that it would exactly specify its alleged rievnnccs, the Diet threatened the Duelti. s wi ll a Federal execution. Urged by the great Bowers, and, like them, anxious to maintain the pea : ot Europe, Denmark, as is well known, made concession- alter concession. The Diet having declared illegal the Constitution of the Danish Monarchy in so far as it regarded the German

Duchies, thereby greatly increased the difficulties in the way of an amicable settlement ; for it could not, without stultifying itself, consent to negotiate, so long as a state of things endured which it had declared invalid. To obviate this difficulty and render an arrangement possible, Denmark made what I think must be admitted to be a great concession. She consented to suspend the impugned Constitution as far as the Duchies were concerned, and it now appears

the ordinances which wore the consequences of that Constitution, as well as that part of the Holstein Constitution which has in like manner been objected to and declared null by the Diet; The question of the domains, to which an undue importance has, chiefly through real bearings, been attached, does not appear to present auy difficulties likely to become serious obstacles to a satisfactory arrangement. Without entering into numerous details which serve hut to complicate the question and render it unpalatable, the above will l think, be found a correct outline sketch of the circumstances of the case. It proves that, as I in former letters have remarked, Denmark, far from showing stubbornness, has displayed the best disposition to

remove, so far as on her depended, all impediments to negotiations with the delegates of the Diet. The object ot those negotiations would he tixdovisc and agree upon the best means of enabling the Duchies to participate in or conform to the common Constitution of Denmark, consistently with a due regard to the requirements of the Federal laws, as well as to the wishes ot the Provincial States of Holstein, which, with L bility of a final and satisfactory arrangement ; seem, then, that there was a fair hope and pro- ttiat view, would be agaiu consulted. It would . hut, unfortunately, the Diet puts forward a pretension which, if insisted upon, threatens again to bring matters to a dead lock. It demands that tire Danish Government should officially communicate to it, before their promulgation, the articles or stipulations which it intends to substitute for those invalidated by the Diet. This : < considered to be an infringement on the so\ ights of the King of Denmark þÿ rights exp, - K iiarantccd by the Federal Act. Aud the del I is the more unpalatable because it docs not appear that compliance with it would answer any useful purpose, but would simply serve as a gratification to tiie vanity of Germany, enabling her to boast that she had made Denmark bend to her will. This ccrtaiuly looks like unnecessary humiliation, and like driving Denmark to the wall. It is ungencreus, and it seems to he unjust. The right of Germany to invalidate þÿ to the extent to which she thought proper to do it þÿ Danish institutions which she

affirmed to he in disaccordance with the Federal laws is open to discussion. Tho Danish Government, desirous to conciliate matters, and also, there is reason to believe, out of deference to the wishes of some of the great Bowers anxious for a settlement of tho question, waived the doubt ns to the extent of the Diet's right. The Diet, for some reason of it own, refused even to specify the exact points to which it objected. Now it says to Denmark, þÿ You shall make changes in the Constitution, and then you shall submit them to our approval before promulgating þÿthem. To this demand Denmark strongly demurs. Compliance faith it would he, it is urged, an abandonment, on the part of the King of Denmark, of his independence, and a waiving of his rights as guaranteed by t the deral Act, which contains no stipulation o justify Fesuch a proceeding. The feeling seems so strong on this point that, if tho Diet insists, it is to he feared tho way lately made towards an amicable arrangement will he again lost, and the affair will once more be seriously embroiled. All these encroachments are believed þÿ I might, perhaps, say are known þÿ to he promoted by Hanover and some other German Governments which have certain objects of their own to curry, and which seek to regain popularity a lost by their own fault. It is to be hoped, however, that the majority of the Diet, uninfluenced by private views, and really desirous to set at rest this troublesome question, will not allow itself to he misled by

such intrigues, but will facilitate the opening of negotiations, without which no satisfactory result can he arrived at. It is much to ho doubted whether Denmark will he induced to make further concessions of any magnitude ; and truly were the great Bowers to take the matter in hand, they could hardly in fairness insist upon more. It is notorious that those already made were far from being approved by public opinion in Denmark, and that they led to the secession from the Danish Cabinet of one of its ablest members, who thought enough had been yielded, more than probable that she will also suspend 1 and that the time had conic to stand firm and prepare for the worst. The public in England and France lias not as yet, T think, taken much heed of this question, and yet it is one that derives interest from the mere fact of the great ignorance of iis ! disproportion of strength between the two parties at issue. The Diet must show itself just and moderate in its demands if it would not see the sympathies of Europe enlisted on the sido of Denmark, which has manifested throughout a moderato and conciliatory disposition. Germany would then, perhaps, regret that she had, by exorbitant demands, prevented the conclusion of a fair and equitable nrrangemont.

70 THU EDITOR OK THE TIMES. Sir, þÿ Having with your kiud permission been enabled to call the attention of dentists to the American discovery of the painless extraction by means of the electric current, I shall feel further obliged if, in answer to my numerous correspondents on that subject, you will allow me through the medium of your columns to make a few observations as to its mode of application. At the time I received the fust information, having by me an electro-maguetic machine, which 1 bad purchased more as a philosophical toy than for any practical purpose, I bought a pennyworth of thin copper wire and set to work. My first experiments were upon poor and ignorant people, who, when asked whether they felt the operation, answered in the affirmative. Not myself recollecting at the time the distinction between sensation and pain, I | tooth extraction. concluded that my experiments were failures, and waited with anxiety the appearance of the

American journal, which I received about the time of the melancholy accident from chloroform at Epsom. I then again set to work in earnest with the same apparatus, and the results were faithfully given in my former letter; from that time I have been inundated with letters from every part of the kingdom and from the continent, inquiring how the new agent was to be applied. With the details of my experiments, which have been many and various, I will not occupy' your space or burden your readers, hut, with your permission, will simply give the results. Any kind of electro-magnetic battery will answer that will produce a smart vibratory motion iu the hands and arms. The patient grasps in one hand a hollow metallic handle attached to one of the poles of the battery, the other pole is attached to the extracting instrument by means of thin copper wire, which cau be twisted and untwisted inslanter , and by wearing a nicely fitting silk glove the operator is perfectly insulated. The following directions also will, I trust, he serviceable : þÿ My present experience shows that the current should not he applied to a tooth with an abscess at the root, to a loose tooth, or to fangs imbedded in spongy gums, as the pain in such cases appears to he increased. When the sides of a tooth arc decayed nearly or quite to the gum, the tooth and surrounding parts should he rendered as dry as possible by means of French bibulous paper ; fangs, when the gums are not spongy, may he extracted with the forceps after

being treated in the same manner. As many of the most scientific men in the kingdom have kindly offered to assist ine in my inquiries, should anything calculated to he of general utility present itself I shall he most happy to make it known through the medium of the dental journals. 1 am, Sir, your obedient servant, JOSEPH SNAPE, Dentist to the Chester Infirmary. Bridge-street, Chester, Sept. 11.

I have since operated upon others with the like result. Because I say the operation is painless, it must not be supposed that I mean pleasant. In fact, the application of the wires from an electric coil and þÿSmec battery, s higher charged than 1J deg., is in itself very painful to the gums and internal mouth. It is therefore an object of much nicety to þÿ regulate the amount of electricity so as to preclude a painless operation becoming a very painful one, either from too much or too little electricity being administered, Tn my own case I felt a bearable amount of electricity when the instrument was placed upon the tooth (underwisdom tooth), hut T found that the same amount applied to the gums over the front teeth was excessively painful. The quantity of electricity that made the operation painless to mo was not enough to kill the sensation of pain in a gentleman for a similar tooth, whereas in a lady shortly after it was quite successful with a less amount. It is hind foot of Ursa Major, and is moving towards Arcturus ; or, in other words, it is near the hori/.ou, and ranging with thi! two stars known as tho pointers, the comet being about as far to the left of the pointers as the North Star is to their right. The tail is tolerably well defined, and about 3 degrees in length. This comet was first discovered on the 2nd of June last by Prof. Douati, in Florence, Italy. It was first seen in this country by Ilcnry M. Parkhurst, of Perth Amboy, N. J , on the 29th of the same month, no information having then been received here of its discovery in Europe. Duo nr two nights afterwards it was discovered by Miss Maria Mitchell, of Nantucket, Mass., who also supposed that it had not previously been seen Thus there were three independent discoveries of this comet, while it was so faint

as only to be visible with a telescope, or about the size of a star of the eleventh magnitude. A very striking characteristic of this comet, when it was first discovered, was its extremely slow motion. In consequence of this slowucss of motion, it was very difficult for astronomers to fix upon its orbit with much accuracy, and there has been considerable difference of opinion upon that subject. The Screw Steam Ship Cleopatra arrived this morning, 38 days from tho Pape, with 378 Chinese emigrants for Havauna. About 70, wo understand, had died on the whole voyage from China, up to her arrival in Carlisle Hay. She puts in here for a supply of coal. By her arrival, we have Cape Town papers of 20th and 25th August, from which we make some extracts. The Small þÿI ox had broken out at Cape Town, amongst the Kaffir population ; which is attributed to the miserable condition of the back streets, aud crowded places, in which they are huddled together, to sleep at night. The Governor, Sir G. Grey, was absent on the frontier, on a mission, to make peace between one of the uative Chiefs, Moshesh, who, with his tribe, arc at war with tho settlers of the Free State and the latter. Several vessels had arrived with German Immigrants. Tho German Legion had not yet settled down in the country, as farmers, but were kept on full pay, and it was said the best thing to do with them, would be to send them on to India, as volunteers. The Elections were being held ; and we notice addresses to gentlemen, to suffisr their names to be proposed for the Legisla-

tive Council ; the Members of which, as well as of the House of Assembly, appear to bo elected by the popular voice. How strange, that a Government, based on the voice of the people, should succeed in South Africa, and yet be impossible in most ot the old aud highly enlightened countries of Europe. The Press is another of their most vigorous institutions. There arc eight Newspapers published in Cape Town, four of which are printed by Steam ; aud not less than sixteen papers published in the Eastern province, which has been more recently settled, and contains a smaller number of inhabitants than the Western, in which Cape Town is situated.

There are now in Cape Town no less than eight newspapers, lour of which are printed by steam. Upon these there must be upwards of sixty printers regularly employed. There are about twenty persons engaged in the literary departments of these eight papers, as editors aud reporters, besides which, each paper keeps its collectors, book keepers, &c. There certainly are not less than one hundred persons in Cape Town who are regularly engaged the whole year through on newspapers. There is one paper alone, which about five years ago, printed but five hundred a week, and had uot more than 300 bona fide subj scribers, that now sells, as we are informed, 1,400 a week. The monthly issue of the Argus, is about 17,000, in addition to supplements; whilst the Mercantile Advertiser, a gratis advertising sheet, has sufficient patronage from advertisers to enable it to j issue, three mornings a week, 2,500 copies. There is a paper issued every day in the week in Cape Town, although there is no daily as yet. The issues are about on Mondays, 3,500 on Tuesdays, 4,100 on Wednesdays, 3,200 on Thursdays, 1,400 (including the Government Gazette) on Fridays, and 5,400 on Saturdays. This makes a total of 21,100 newspapers issued in Cape Town every week, in addition to supplements. To day, for the English mail, the Argus will issue nearly 2,000 sheets, including its regular monthly summary. The press of Cape Town supplies the whole of the Western Province with news. There is no paper published in any West-

ern town except Cape Town. Whilst the older province (the Western) has only eight papers, the Eastern Province, which is the most sparely populated, and the youngest, has twice that number. There are seven papers published in þÿGraham Town, s three in Port Elizabeth, two in Graff-Reinet, one in Albert, two in King þÿWilliam Town, s and one in Gradock. Immigration is going on, but we shall soon be overdone with skilled labor. Blacksmiths and carpenters are very necessary, but they are only consumers, and do not aid much in developing the resources of the country. We want more agricultural laborers. Wool is increasing daily in amount and improving in quality ; but wheat, the staff of life, and other cereals and necessaries of life, are grown to a ludicrously small extent in a country capable of any amount of production. We want more producers, for we have still to draw the most of our supplies of food from foreign sources. Slavery on the west coast is rampant, as indeed, it seems to be everywhere just now. The capture of a Portuguese supposed slave cutter is affording employment at present to the Mixed Commission. We are much in want of a Civil Engineer to supply the official vacancy which has occurred. It is hoped that a really efficient man will bo sent out, and not a mere hanger-on of the Colonial Office. Fifty-two thousand pounds, a large sum for us, has been voted for new roads and bridges during the present year. A great deal of our future progress in necessary public works
depends upon having an engineer properly up to his work. Railways and other works, not provided for iu tho above sum, will also bo commenced this year.

Correspondence of the N. Y. Express. Apprehended Difficulty between Paraguay and England. Buenos Ayres, July 30, 1858. People hope here that the American Expedition will hurry up. If the United States Go- ! vernment should delay much longer, there will be none of Paraguay left ; for Lopez seems determined to run himself into the jaws of as many lions as possible, as if just to see how often he can make a hair-breadth escape from annihilation. This time ho has aroused the ire of the British Lion, and if Her þÿMajesty Miuister s is as spunky 1 as he has the credit of being, Lopez may have an English war on his hands, before he is called upon to settle for his outrages upon Americans. | The facts of the case are as follows þÿ as nearly as I can gather. Mr. Christie, the British Minister near the Argentine Confederation, started some weeks since for Paraguay on board II. B þÿM. steamer s Wasp, for the purpose, it is supposed, of renewing the English treaty, which expires this year, or of making a better one in its stead. The Wasp broke down, her propeller becoming deranged, and sho had to return to this port; whereupon Mr. Christie took passage on tho Paraguayan merchant steamer Salto de Guayra, and proceeded in safety to Asuuction. Soon after his arrival, be opened negotiations, and as a preliminary step waited upon llis Excellency, the President, to present his credentials. At his first visit be found Lopez dressed in a preposterous costume, half military, half di- I

plomatic, and some parts of it so grossly exaggerated as to make it extremely ridiculous. To complete his uniform, Lopez wore an immense cocked hat all fringed with þÿswan d s own, bedizened with gold lace ; and this ornament he persisted in keeping upon his head during the whole interview, at which discourtesy Mr. Christie took serious umbrage, as he is most unyielding 1 in matters of etiquette. He retired from the interview rather abruptly, and made official complaint of the affront the President had put upon Her þÿMajesty Minister s by wearing his bat at an official interview, whereupon its sapient Paraguayan Secretary replied to the indignant plenipotentiary that Her Majesty, the Queen, always wore her crown and robes of state when she received foreign ministers, and that the President of Paraguay saw no impropriety in wearing his hat, which with him took the place of the peculiar ensign of royalty disported by the Queen. Mr. Christie asked for his passports, and without delay took passage on a small English merchant steamer called the Little Polly, owned and loaded by the English house of Gettings, of this city. When some thirty or forty leagues below Asuncion, the Little Polly met the Paraguayan war steamer Tacuari. It was night time when they sighted each other and both vessels had lights up. The Tacuari, without making signals of any kind, deliberately altered her course, and ran plump into the Little Polly, cutting her down to the þÿwater edge. s It is estimated here, that the Tacuari people
as Mr. had no idea that so distinguished a Christie was of board on tho Little dignitary

Her only intention was to cripple the Little Polly, because the vessel interfered with the traffic of the Salto de Guayra, Ypora, and other steamers owned by Lopez, which virtually monopolize the steam trade of the river. However, this time the Paraguayans have caught a Tartar. Last year the Tacuari ran deliberately into the French war steamer Bisson, while that vessel was lying at anchor, for which outrage Lopez had to make an humble apology, and disburse $10,000. This case is much more serious, as the steamer and the whole of her valuable cargo are totally lost, and are not insured. Nobody supposes that Mr. Christie, who has returned to Parana, will rest satisfied with so inglorious a termination of his mission to Paraguay. The Brazilian steamer Mage, the supposed loss of which I communicated in my last, has turned up þÿ considerably battered by bad weather, but without loss of life. She has put back into Santa Catalina, where she still remains. President Lopez therefore, has not yet to deplore the loss of his son, Bcnigo, who was a passenger on board of the Mage The question now recurs where did the dead bodies in Brazilian uniform, reported as seen by vessels bound to this port, come from ?

SPAIN. A Royal order, countersigned by Marshal þÿO Donncl as Minister of War, has been published directing the concentration at Cadiz of the body of troops to he scut to the Isle of Cuba, and to form a portion of the forces sent to Mexico in ease redress should not he given to the Spanish subjects who have of late had to suffer from the violent measures of the Mexican Government, and satisfaction afforded to Spain for the murders committed some time ago. The Gazette contains the long-expected declaration of the policy to be pursued by Marshal þÿO Donneland his colleagues . This declaration is in the form of a circular addressed to the governors of the provinces by the Minister

of the Interior: þÿ þÿ After informing them that the Queen by the advice of her Ministers, has dissolved the Chamber of Deputies, and directed a new one to be elected and convoked, the circular states that the Cabinet thinks it expedient to govern the country conformably to the Constitution of 1845. The Ministers arc determined to proceed with the desamortisation of ecclesiastical property, in order to develop the weal ill and perfect the administration of the country. They will introduce important municipal reforms, and constitute the provinces in such a manner as to give them more administrative independence, without, however, deadening the tutelar action of the supreme Government. The time is come for some decentralisation in the administration of the country. The Ministers wish to establish trial by jury for all offences that have reference to questions that may be objects of public discussion, and thus the judges are not obliged to take too much part in the ardent political disputes of the day. The Cabinet will give all its attention to the material interests of the country. The Government will not countenance the tendencies of those who are for ever dreaming of giving the constitutional monarchy new bases and untried modifications, and who would administer the country with the help of a set of officials exclusively chosen from one class only of public men. The Ministers arc of opinion that parties of this kiud do not deserve the name of constitutional, nor do they

believe that the country can obtain from them any other result than anarchy or despotism. The Governors will, therefore, accept the cooperation of all candidates who associate honestly with the Cabinet in carrying out Constitutional Government. They will consider the denominations of candidates as of no importance, provided that their opinions concerning the Constitution, the dynasty, and the principal political questions are in accordance with those of her þÿMajesty s present Ministers. In conclusion, the Ministers expect that the governors of provinces will not impose candidates upon electoral districts, nor demand the systematic exclusion of any class of political men, nor consent to any transgression of the laws that may cast a stain upon the solemn impartiality of this great constitutional act which is about to take þÿplace.

The solution of the difficulty, according to the Journal des Debats, has been found in the system of a regency, The King has decided to give his brother the regency of the kingdom, and the Prince oi will cepted it. This arrangement Prussia has ac- not prevent the resumption of full powers by the King, should his Majesty at any future time recover his physical and mental health ; but the Prince of Prussia, in the meantime, will lie altogether untrammelled in the exercise of his duties as Regent. T'hcso regulations produced such a bad impres-
sion on the public that the Gavcrnmcnt has thought it advisable to order the director of police to withdraw them.
ITALY. SARDINIA. The Courrier da Dimanche gives the following analysis of a circular addressed by Count de Cavour to the representatives of Piedmont at Foreign Courts, on the occasion o! the cession

s lu c ff Oj I) & Y o SU to the Russian Steam Company of certain buildings in the port of Villafranca : þÿ þÿ The Cabinet of Turin commences by declaring that the concession to Russia of the old convict establishment is gratuitous and temporary ; that the premises are to be transformed into a depot for fuel and stores. The Sardinian Minister complains subsequently of the ill-intentioned reflections of the English press, which accused Sardinia of having ceded one of its best ports to Russia, to the detriment of her own interest and of those of England. Count do Cavour calls the attention of the Sardinian diplomatic authorities to a note in the Piedmontese Gazette, re-establishing the facts which had been misrepresented by illinformed correspondents. By that explanation, as well as by what was written by the Piedmontese Legation when the French Government was questioned as to the request of Russia, it is evident that there has been no cession of the port of Villafranca ; that the pretended cession is restricted to the gratuitous concession, liable to be revoked at a determined moment, and to the use of the convict establishment at Villafranca, long unoccupied. The Minister cites the pr cedent of a similar concession to the Unit States in the Gulf of Spczzia. Agreed to many years ago, that concession is still in force ; aud no objection has been made on the poiut by foreign journals. Finally, Count de Cavour concludes by recommending to the representatives of Piedmont in foreign countries to rectify, in
conformity with his circular, the facts with reference to which they may happen to be interrogated in the course of conversation with statesþÿmen.

NAPLES. A letter from Naples, dated f pt. 22, gives a dispatch from Count Carat > t Prince Petrulla, Neapolitan Minister at Vienna, in reply to insecret negotiations quiries from Count with and the þÿTuileries : þÿ Buol relative to þÿ þÿ the Court.- of St. þÿJames s The King, our august pretended master, has never derogated from l is duty for anybody or anything, in any circumstances. and Con- strained, contrary to his will, by lorce violence, to submit to acts against which reason and law protest, he may have been ; but these acts will never have the sanction of his conscience, and his Majesty will always consider them as an outrage to his sacred person, agaiust which he has no means of reacting. The heart of his Majesty knows not forgetfulness. His Majesty was profoundly wounded when to without reason, contrary France and England, international law, and for causes which were in reality only pretexts, withdrew their Ministers from his Court. Having been thus offended, and the offence not having been mitigated by the subsequent conduct of the two Powers, his Sicilian Majesty would consider himself humiliated in his own eyes, in the eyes of his subjects aud of Europe, if lie took any steps to bring about a reconciliation. When the representatives of the two Courts resided here, all the movements of the Governments were watched, scanned, and measured, and each to an investigation independent act of as its sovereignty annoying as it was wound- was subjected ing. Since the Government has been freed from

this interference and unjustifiable control, its movements have been more free, more rapid, and the happy subjects of his Majesty have reaped the benefits of the change. . . . All that passed, all that was said at Cherbourg on this subject, in no way affects us ; lor nothing has been done or said at our suggestion, but probably as a result of the desire expressed at the Court of England by the Powers friendly to our Sovereign, and principally by Prussia and Bavaria. This does not imply, however, that a reconciliation with the two European Powers would not be very agreeable to us ; but as it was not the King who caused this rupture, so it will not be by the King that the first steps towards reconciliation arc þÿtaken. The King, we are told, no longer admits fruit to his table, for the report has been spread that bombs, iu the shape of pears, peaches, ij-c., have been manufactured. Nay, suspicion goes so far that sweetmeats even are suspected, and the confectioners receive unnumbered visits from the police in order that it may be seen whether the jam, <5-0., they use is or is not fulminating powder. Everything that comes from abroad is submitted to a ridiculous examination ; the King can get no sleep, it is said, and his health is suffering. Fresh arrests have been made at Naples as the result of a mysterious discovery. On the

beach at Miseuo a dead body was recently found. It was that of a traveller, it appears, who, in order to avoid examination by the police and the Custom-house at Naples, hud attempted to swim across the strait of Procida. The political Lcander sunk, for the strait is wide and dangerous. The police found upon him papers of grave importance, and thus obtained the clue to a plot of immense proportions. A vast number of arrests were immediately made amongst the nobility-, the naval and military officers, aud the upper bourgooisio. An army of policemen has been dispatched into the provinces, in order to complete the razzia.

THE CHINESE TREATY. The following is an official summary- of the treaty between her Majesty and the Emperor of China, signed at Ticnt-sin, Juno 2G, IS58: þÿ Art. 1. Confirms the treaty of Nankin of 1812, and abrogates tho supplementary- treaty and general regulations of trade. Art. 11. Provides for the appointment of Ambassadors, Ministers, or other diplomatic agents ion the part of either country at the Court of Pekin and St. þÿJames s. Art. III. Contains provisions for tho permanent establishment of a British Minister, his family aud suite at Pekin, and the forms to be observed in his communications with the Imperial Government. Art. þÿIV . Makes arrangements for the travelling and tho transmission of the correspondence of the Minister and the employment by him of special couriers. Art. V. The Emperor of China consents to nominate one of tho Secretaries of State, or some high officer, to transact business with the British Minister, either personally or in writing, on a footing of perfect equality. Art. VI. The same privileges are to be granted to the Chinese Minister in London. Art. VII. Consuls may be appointed in China, and may reside in any of the open ports, and their official rank and position as regards the Chinese local authorities is determined. Art. VIII. The Christian rcli; -ion, ns professed by Protestants or Roman Catholics, to be tolerated, and its professors protected. Art. IX. British subjects to travel for pleasure or trade into all parts of the interior, with passports from their Consuls, countersigned

by the local authorities. The regulations as regards these passports arc determined. The provisions of the article not to be applied to tho þÿships crews, for the due restraint of whom regulations are to bo drawn up by the Consul and the local authorities. No pass to bo given to Nankin, or cities in the hands of the rebels. Art. X. British merchant-ships arc to be allowed to trade up the great river (Yang-tsz), but in the present disturbed state of the Upper and Lower Valley-, no port is to be opened lor trade, with the exception of Chin Kiang, which is to be opened in a year from the signature of the treaty. When pence is restored, British i vessels are to be admitted to trade at such ports, as far as Hankow, not exceeding three iu number, as the British Minister, after consulting with the Chinese. Secretary of State, shall determine.

Art. XI. In addition to the present ports New Cliwang, Tang Chow, Tai Wan (Formosaj, Chow Chow (Swatow), and Kiung-Chow (Hainan), are to be opened, and the right of residence and holding landed property is conceded. Art. XII. British subjects are to make agreements for landed property at the rates prevailing aiRong the people. Art. XIII. No restrictions to be placed on the employment by British subjects of Chinese subjects in any lawful capacity. Art. XIV. The hire of boats for transport of goods or passengers to be settled between the parties themselves, without the interference of the Chinese Government. The number of boats not to be limited, and no monopoly allowed. If any smuggling takes place, the offenders to be punished according to law. Art. XV. All questions in regard to rights of property or person between British subjects to be subject to the jurisdiction of the British authorities. Art. XVI. Chinese subjects guilty of any criminal acts towards British subjects to be arrested and punished by the Chinese authorities according to the law of China ; British subjects committing any crime in China to be tried and punished by the Consul or other public functionary according to the laws of Great Britain. Art. XV II. Determines the mode of procedure in the matter of complaints on the side either of British or Chinese subjects. Art. XVIII. Provides for the protection of the persons and property of British subjects. Art. XIX. If any British merchant vessel in Chinese waters is plundered by robbers or

pirates the Chinese authorities are to use every endeavour to capture and punish the offenders, aud to recover the stolen property. Art. XX. Wrecked or stranded vessels, or vessels under stress of weather, are to be afforded relief and security in any Chinese port; and the crews are to be furnished by the Chinese, il necessary, with the means of conveyance to the nearest consular station. in Hong Kong, or on board of British refuge Art. XXI. Chinese criminals taking ships, shall, upon the requisition of the Chinese authorities, be given up, the same also if taking refuge in the houses, or on board the vessels of British subjects at the open ports. Art. XXII. The Chinese authorities to do their utmost to arrest Chinese subjects failing to discharge their debts to British subjects or fraudulently absconding, aud to enforce recovery of the debts. The British authorities to do likewise as regards British subjects indebted to Chinese. Art. XXIII. Debts incurred by Chinese at Hong Kong must be recovered in the Courts of Justice on the spot. If the debtor should abscond, and should possess real or personal property in the Chinese territory, the Chinese authorities, in concert with the British Consul, are to see justice done between the parties. Art. XXIV. British subjects shall pay on all merchandise imported or exported, the duties prescribed by the tariff, but in no case shall they pay other or higher duties than the subjects of other foreign nations pay. Art. XXV. Import duties to be considered

payable on the landing of the goods and duties of export on the shipment of the same. Art. XXVI. The tariff fixed by Articlo X. of the treaty of Nankin to be revised by a commission of British and Chinese officers, to meet at Shanghai, so that the revisod tariff may come into operation immediately after the ratification of the treaty. Art. XXVII. Either contracting party may demand a further revision of the tariff and of the commercial articles of the treaty at the end of 10 years; but six þÿmonths notice must be given, or the tariff is to remain in force for 10 years more, and so at the end of each successive 10 years. Art. XXVtII. It is agreed that within four months of the signature of the treaty, the Chinese collector of duties at ports already opened and hereafter to be opened to British trade, shall bo obliged, on application of tho Consul, to declare the amount of duties leviable on produce between the place of production and the port of shipment, anil upou imports between the consular port in question aud the inland markets named

S f B n 0 I X A V I S ._ by the Consul ; and a notification thereof shall be published in English and Chinese. British subjects may, however, clear their goods of all transit duties by payment of a single charge, the amount of the charge to bo calculated as near as possible at the rate of two-and-a-half per cent. ad valorem duty, and it is to be fixed for each article at the Conference to be held at Shanghai. The payment of transit dues by commutation is in no way to affect the tariff duties on imports or exports, which will continue to be levied separately and in full. Art. XXIX. Regulates the amount of tonnage dues. British merchant vessels of more than 150 tons burden to pay at the rate of 4 mace per ton; if of 150 tons and under, at the rate of 1 mace per ton. Vessels engaged in the coasting trade, or clearing for Hong Kong from any of the open ports, shall be entitled to a special certificate exempting them from all further payment of tonnage dues in any open port of China for a period of four months from the date of her port clearance. Art. XXX. The master of any British merchant-vessel may within 48 hours after his arrival, but not later, depart without breaking bulk ; in which ease he will not be subject to pay tonnage dues. No other fees or charges upon entry or departure shall be levied. Art. XXXI. No tonnage dues to be paid on passenger boats, or boats conveying baggage, letters, articles of provision, or other articles not subject to duty. All cargo boats, however, conveying merchandise subject to duty, shall pay

tonnage dues once in six months, at the rato of lour mace per registered ton. Art. XXXII. The Consuls and Superintendents of Customs to consult together respecting the erection of buoys and lightships, as occasion may demand. Art. XXXIII. Duties to be paid to the authorised Chinese bankers, either in syce or in foreign money, according to the assay made at Canton, July 13, 1843. Art. XXXIV. Sets of standard weights and measures to be delivered by the Superintendent of Customs to the Consul at each part, to secure uniformity. Art. XXXV. British merchant-vessels to bo at liberty to engage pilots to take them into any of the open ports, and to convey them out, after they have discharged all legal dues and duties. Art. XXXVI. The Superintendent of Customs shall depute one or more Customs officers to guard a British merchant-ship on arriving off one of the open ports. They shall stay either in a boat of their own or on board ship ; their food and expences shall be supplied from the Custom-house, and they shall be entitled to no fees from the master or consignee. Art. XXXVII. þÿShips papers, bills of lading, <)-c., to be lodged in the bauds of the Consul 24 hours after arrival, and full particulars of the vessel to be reported to the Superintendent of Customs within a further period of 24 hours ; omission to comply with this rule within 48 hours punishable by a fine of 50 taels for each þÿday s delay. The total amount of penalty not to exceed 200 taels. The master responsible for

the correction of the manifest; a false manifest subjects the master to a fine of 500 taels, but he will be allowed to correct any mistake within 24 hours, without incurring the penalty. . Art. XXXVIII. If the master shall begin to discharge any goods without the permit from the Superintendent of Customs he shall be fined 500 taels, and the goods discharged shall be confiscated wholly. Art, XXXI X. British merchants must apply to the Superintendent of Customs for a special permit to land or ship cargo. Cargo landed or shipped without such permit will be liable to confiscation. Art. XL. No trans-shipment from one vessel to another can be made without special permission, under pain of confiscation of the goods trans-shipped. Art. xu. The Superintendent of Customs shall give a port clearance when all dues and duties have been paid, and the Consul shall then return the þÿship papers. s Art. xtii. If the British merchant cannot agree with the Chinese officer in fixing a value on goods subject to an ad valorem duty, each party shall call in two or three merchants, and the highest price at which any of the merchants would purchase them shall be assumed to be tho value of the goods.

Art. xuit. Provides that duties shall be charged upon the net weight of each article, making a deduction for the tare weight of congee, to., and regulates the manner in which the tare on any article such as tea shall be fixed. The British merchant may appeal to his Consul within 24 hours. Art. xuv. Upon all damaged goods a fair reduction of duty shall be allowed, proportionate to their deterioration. If any disputes arise, they shall be settled in the manner pointed out in the clause of this treaty having reference to articles which pay duty ad, valorem. Art. xlv. British merchants who have imported merchandise into an open port and paid duty, may reimport their goods under certain regulations, without payment of any additional duty. British merchants desiring to re-export duty-paid imports to a foreign country to be entitled, under similar regulations, to a drawbackcertificate, which is to be a valid tender in payment of Customs duties. Foreign grain brought into a Chinese port in a British ship, if no part has been landed, may be re-exported without hindrance. Art xlvi . The Chinese authorities at tho ports to adopt the means they may judge most proper to prevent the revenue suffering from fraud or smuggling. Art. xlvii. British merchant-vessels not to resort to other than tho ports declared open ; not unlawfully to enter ports or to carry on clandestine trade along the coasts. Vessels violating this provision to be, with their cargoes, subject to confiscation by the Chinese Government.

Art. xlvii i. If a British merchant-vessel be concerned in smuggling, the goods to be subject to confiscation by the Chinese authorities, aud the ship may be prohibited from trading further, and sent away as soon as her accounts shall have been adjusted. Art. xi.ix. All penalties or confiscations under the treaty to belong and be appropriated to the public service of the Chinese Government. Art. i.. All official communications addressed by British diplomatic or consular agents to the Chinese authorities are henceforth to be written in English. For the present they will be accompanied by a Chinese version, but it difference that in case of there being any is understood of meaning between the English and Chinese text, the English Government will hold the sense expressed in the English text to be the correct sense. This provision is to apply to the present treaty, the Chinese text of which has been carefully corrected by tho English original. Art. li. The character þÿ þÿI ('barbarian) not to be applied to the British Government or to British subjects in any Chinese official documents issued by the Chinese authorities. Art. lii. British ships of war coming for no hostile purpose, or being engaged in the pursuit of pirates, to be at liberty to visit all the Chinese ports and receive every facility for procuring necessaries, or, if required, for making repairs. The commanders of such ships to hold intercourse with the Chinese authorities on terms of equality and courtesy. Art. Liu. The contracting parties agree to

concert measures for the suppression of piracy. Art. Li v. Confirms all advantages secured to the British Government by previous treaties, and stipulates that the British Government shall parby the Emperor of China to any ticipate in any advantages which other may be grauted nation. Art. t.v. The conditions affecting indemnity for expenses incurred and loss sustain d in tho matter of the Canton question to be included in a separate article, which shall be in every respect of equal validity with the other articles of the treaty. Art. lvi. Ratifications to be exchanged within a year after the day of signatures. Separate article provides that a sum of two millions of taels, on account of the losses sustained by British subjects through the misconduct of tho Chinese authorities at Canton ; and a further sum of two millions of taels on account of the expenses of the war shall be paid to the British representative in China by the authorities of the Kwang Tung province. The arrangements for effecting these payments to bo determined by the British representative in concert with the Chinese authorities at Kwang Tung. The British forces arc not to be withdrawn from Canton until the above amounts are discharged in full.

Consecration of the Moravian Church at Nisky, On Sunday last (17th instant) the ceremony of consecrating the new Moravian Church at the settlement of Nisky, in the west-end quarter of the Island took place. The building consists

of a fine stone basement, intended to serve as a School Room, and capable of accommodating some two hundred scholars; the system of teaching to be observed there being, we believe, that which is known as the Mico method. The second story is built entirely of wood, aud when seen at a little distance with its roof and sides painted in mild and subdued colours, a neat belfry at the top of the eastern gable, with a vane surmounting the same, lias on the whole a good aud pleasing appearance, whilst its gothic shaped windows informs the stranger on his approach that he is in the vicinity of a Church. The building stands directly east and ivest, and the Church is entered at the South by ascending at the east and west two flights of brick steps erected in a semi-circle shape, and brings you at the same time to a large platform in the rear þÿ the whole seemingly arranged to answer the local position of the site, and contiguous with the dwellings wherein the Ministers reside. The interior of the Church, as a rule, it would seem, with all the Moravian Churches here, is exceedingly plain, but neverthelcss arranged with neatness and a due regard to the convenience of the congregation when assembled ; whilst the situation assures the visitor that it is healthy and will l>e cool and airy during service. The arrangements comprise a neatly painted Pulpit made of deal, a well toned Seraphinc and plain benches without backs, placed out in rows to scat about GOO persons. It might be proper that wo should

say that the Moravian Churches, of which there arc three on the Island þÿ one in the eastend (Ncivhernhut), one in the town, and the third, of which this article treats, .and built at Nisky þÿ down, arc, for the most part, intended for the to replace an old one recently taken rural populations to worship in ; hut as the so termed rural populations have, to an extraordinary degree, become eity þÿfolk within Lite þÿ years, largo groups of well clad persons might have been seen from an early hour on Sunday morning leaving the town aud going westward. The membersof the congregation shewed every disposition to render the ceremony as iutcivsting as possible, and in consequence (for sonic days previous to the event,) a commencement was made to decorate the Church, and flowers in abundance, along with evergreens were hung in festoons and other ornamental design-, as well as cakes and other refreshments, provided to celebrate the occasion on the subsequent day. The Reverend Professor C. 11, Goetz, one of the Missionary Brothers at St. Croix, came over purposely to officiate at the ceremony. The þÿRov d, gentleman took for his text þÿ Revelations, chap. xxi. vs. 3. In the course of his discourse he rendered a short but interesting account of the þÿ United þÿBrethren, sent forth as a Missionary Body to christianize the heathen or untutored inhabitants of these Islands at the period of their early settlement, and proceeded to show the rise and progress from the advent of their coming to the present

period ; and we believe it is not more than is due to them to say that, in all time have they amply fulfilled their mission. The ceremony from the beginning to the conclusion was conducted in an orderly and becoming manner, although the number of persons present, owing to the congregations of the other Churches having come to participate tjiciciu, made it impossible for the Church to accommodate the whole, and many were therefore obliged to remain outside.

Vessel Foundered. By an arrival from N'aguabo, P. R., we learn the arrival at llutnacao on Saturday afternoon (IGth,) at 5 þÿo clock, in an open boat, of Capt. James Hassei., the mate and crew (G in number) of the British Schooner Water Witch, 54 tons, of Antigua. þÿ4 he Water Witch left this port on Friday afternoon (15th) at 4 þÿo clock, in ballast, bound to Maracaibo, where she was proceeding to procure a cargo of coffi c and corn, and the Capt. had with him one hnndred and twenty doubloons or $1,920, for the purchase of the same. A letter from Naguabo states that at half past 11 þÿo clock, of the night the schooner left here without any appearance of squall þÿ she ivas struck by what must be supposed a tornado or whirlwind, and in less than two seconds went down, the boat and crew remaining on the surface of the water. From the London Times , October 1. SPAIN. A private lettor from Corunna, of the 23(1, rays : þÿ þÿ You will have seen that the Cortes are at length dissolved, and that the decree is dated Corunna, 11th inst. When I wrote on the 15th 1 was not aware that þÿO Donnell, when he left Corunna on the night of the lltli, to preede the Queen in her journey to Lugo, had the important decree in his pocket. He had a h long interview with Her Majesty before he left, and I now learn that it was signed that night, and that þÿO Donnell had permission not to wait for her at Lugo, but to proceed direct to Madrid, where he arrived on the night of the 13th, to, it appears, the no small surprise of his colleagues, ns ho ordered that his approach to the capital should not bo telegraphed, i tun assured that he arrived just in time to counteract a plan hatched at Madrid to oust him from power, in which it is whispered some of his colleagues were more or less concerned. It was notorious at Corunna that lie was not on good terms either with the Minister of State (Foreign Affairs) or the Minister of Marine during the þÿQueen stay s here, and I have some reason to suspect that they did not know the Queen had signed the decree for the dissolution of the Cortes on the night of the 11th. It was stated by certain persons in the antechamber of the Palace, while waiting to take leave of the Queen on the 12ih, that the dissolution would not be decided till the Court reached Madrid. You will draw your own conclusions from these facts. For my own part, I appre-

hend that þÿO Donnell's Administration, at least as it is at pivent constituted, is in a precarious þÿcondition. þÿ A Ministerial crisis is for the twccntictli time spoken of. I rather think it is permanent, and that before long changes will bo made in the Cabinet. M. Mon is paying his farewell vi.-its preparatory to sotting out for Paris. Five magistrates and the President of tho Royal Tribunal of Cuba have been dismissed for certain reasons, which arc only whispered, but m t openly þÿavowed. A letter from lleyrouf, of the 16th inst., describes the country throughout Syria to be in a stale ol great agitation. There arc continual disturbances in many localities, the Turkish (Jovernnicut exercising scarcely any authority in that province, where the Christian populations live in pcrpctunl fear of the Mussulmans. The roads in Syria are unsafe for travellers, in consequence of the number of brigands who infest them. They advance to the very gates of tlie towns, and when any are captured they escape unpunished. The Emir Kalil, son of the Kaimakau, was attacked by a band of robbers on passing the river, and owed his escape solely to the number of his escort.
