Among the many remedial measures which have been boasted of in tbo public prints during the last two years, as about to be tried in the kingdom of the Two Sicilies, were the provincial commissions Tho uninitiated drew a beautiful picture of experienced independent men, intent on correcting abuses, and giving an impetus to tho awakened energies of the inhabitants. þÿ Of course that was tho right way to go to work, and a monarch, more father than king, had at last suggested the right method of regenerating the þÿkingdom. And so the commissions, after long delay, went forth, and though no publicity is ever given to any thing in Naples except the establishment of a new fair, or the celebration of a religious or Royal fete, still some details have crept out regarding tho results of some of theso commissions at least. Among the commissioners for the Calabrias was Signor Gallotti, a man of probity, who seemed disposed to inspect minutely and to report honestly, and in such a

« T . c n o i x a\ v n s « spirit I hear he drew up his report and þÿ destroyed it. The inference is, that he feared to j months ago, the Prince expressly declared that tell the truth. We can understand that timi- i ho would hold it but for one year. That period dity in be this country, can brought to ruin the man who renders where so many influences himself obnoxious, but the fact speaks volumes as to the state of tho province and as to tho interest which exists to conceal the truth. Bolder than Gallotti was another commissioner called Ioccha, a councillor of the Supreme Court, who drew up his report to the King and presented it. It was, say my nil' mints, in the same sense with that of G dlot and must have revealed some disagrecao .ffensivo truths. Ioccha was denounce I as mad and lost his Office, and the other commissioners reported þÿ ail þÿwell. Like the fox iu the fable, they had learnt prudence from the misfortunes of their companion in hunting. They cared not to come under the claws of the lion. The whole story is suggestive, and it shows how strong an interest there is in concealing abuses, how great the danger in exposing them, how little real energy is employed in enforcing investigation, and how þÿ the better. Theso provincial þÿcommissions j hopeless is any change for | were, you will remember, one of the several vaunted measures brought forward soon after the withdrawal of the Legations, and intended to show that at length the Government was resolved to enter on reforms. My report would

be incomplete, say my informants, were I not to state that Ioccha, in bis report, quoted some of the inhabitants of Barlctta as authorities tor the truth of his statements, that some of these were imprisoned, and are still in prison. Ot course, 1 do not give the above report on my own certain knowledge, but on the information of those whom 1 have, generally found trustworthy, yet similar cases may be found widely scattered over the country. From the Illustrated London News, Oct. 2, 1858. Some of our daily contemporaries have announced as positive the abdication of tho King of Prussia. But the announcement is premature. That the King ought to have abdicated, or that the persons about him should have recommended that course mouths ago, is now but too obvious to all Prussia þÿ the Ministerial party excepted þÿ reason to hope and believe that and to all who take any interest in the general affairs of Europe. The þÿKing s malady þÿ a softening of the brain þÿ is fast reducing him to a state of idiotcy; and for the personal comfort of the unhappy Monarch, if his immediate attendants and custodians have any pity or humanity, he ought to be withdrawn from the glare of publicity iu which he is still kept, and consigned for tho remainder of his days to that strict privacy and tender solicitude which his health demands, and which, in the case of a less illustrious individual, would long since have been accorded to one so hopelessly afflicted. But as a formal abdication is a legal act, which a person iu tho þÿKing sunhappy position, is not competent to perform, it is most probable that, as iu the similar case of George 111. with us, there will be no abdication, and that the King will remain to tho cud of his days the titular sovereign of Prussia. An article of the Prussian Constitution provides for tho circumstances that have arisen by declaring a Regency to be established de jure in the event of the þÿsovereign i s ncapacity ; but as this incapacity, though well known, has not been

formally notified, either by medical or legal authority, a middle course has been adopted, at variance witli tho spirit, if not with tho letter, of the Constitution. The Prince of Prussia, been declared Vicar of the Kingdom a position instead of being appointed to the Regency, has þÿ in which ho has not the same powers that be would have if invested with tho Regency. On

accepting this inferior position, more than eleven expires on the 23rd instant, at or before which time a struggle must take place in Prussia for the decision of this great question, which revolves itself into this þÿ whether the þÿ þÿKreuz-parthoi, the despotic, anti-Libcral faction which now surrounds the unfortunate King, shall succeed in prolonging the present anomalous condition of affairs by the appointment of a new Vicar, or whether tho Prince of Prussia shall succeed to tho Regency, and to the full powers which belong to it ? A year ago tho Prince was naturally, though perhaps impolitically, averse from taking any step which might have seemed to imply in his own mind the belief that the malady of the King, his brother, was at that time incurable ; but tho circumstances both of the King and the country have changed in the interval. The last glimmer of hope of the þÿKing recovery s has died away ; and the Vicarship, with its qualified and restricted powers, has been found prejudicial to the public interest. The Liberal party, strong in tho Chambers, has been deterred by the personal influence and advice of the Prince from taking that action on the subject to which its feelings, no less than its principles and the strict requirements of the Constitution, would have otherwise impelled it. Every one will sympathise with the motives of the Prince in not desiring to expedite a crisis, when his personal ambition might appear to be at variance with fraternal affection. But in postponing his direct action for a whole year, the Prince has paid

sufficient respect to natural leo'iijg ; and, at the end of tho time fixed by himself the proper machinery of the Legislature must bo allowed to come into legitimate operation, and to decide once for all the question of the actual Sovereignty of the kingdom of Prussia. The Kreuz-parthoi þÿ the party who wish to drive backwards the wheels of the State machine ; to undo all that has been done for the constitutional liberties of tho people within the last ten years; to maximize the authority of the King; and to minimize, if they cannot entirely destroy, the action of the Parliamentary system þÿ will doubtless die hard in the approaching conflict. But there can bo no doubt as to the ultimate result. The Prince of Prussia will in all probability, in the course of nature, very shortly succeed to the throne ; but iu that interval, whether it be long or short, it is for the iutcrcst of good government iu Prussia þÿ and we may say for that of all Europe þÿ that the Prince should cease to hold his present exceptional position and assume that which the constitution of the State, and his personal consanguinity to the King, us well as political justice and ucccssity, entitle him. Prussia has lost influence and prestige under the weak and vacillating rule of þÿ the man of good þÿintentions, whose mind has given way under a responsibility too great for it to bear ; and there is every the new Sovereign, whether Regent King, will help to as or restore her to a more dignified position in the
councils of Europe, and to one more consistent with tho prosperity and liberty of the people, both of Prussia and of all Germany that is not Austrian.

Madame Ilistori has been playing a character at Venice in which she had to enunciate a sentiment of hostility to an armed oppression by foreigners. Tbc audience caught it up, and applying it of course to Austria, thundered their applause till the house rang again, and then encored the passage. But encores are not permitted in the happy lands of tho South until a man in uniform, appointed by the State, has been consulted as to whether an aria or a duet may be repeated ; and this fellow was not in his place when Madame Ristori left the stage to ask his permission, nor could lie be found- The audience were stormy and clamorous, and at last the actress went back and repeated the words, with the original electrical result. When the official did appear, lie is stated to have used abusive language to the artiste, and to have threatened to imprison her.

COM MUNICATIONS. þÿCliristiaiisteri Churchyard. s There are undoubtedly but few of the inhabitants of this town, who have not some dear relations or friends buried in the Churchyard, and we are certainly not few in number, who do not feel inclined now and then to visit the last retiring-place of our beloved deceased. But in what condition is this resting-place at present A complete grass-piece, where the visitor only discovers from the ruined monuments, that it is a Cemetery. T lit re is no i shade whatever, and in the mornings, when peace and solemnity invite us to visit the graves of our departed, the high damp grass with which the path-ways are overgrown, prevents us from doing so, especially ladies ; consequently these inconvenicncies render it almost impossible to gratify our desire. Now the question is : þÿ ought not and could not a change be effected þÿ1 The author of these lines docs not wish to put his fellow citizens to any expense, nor does he propose making out of it either a þÿ Pi-re la þÿchaise or an þÿ Assistents þÿKirkegaard, but merely wishes to see it altered into a pleasing and comfoiting place and at tho same time an agreeable walk for visitors, which couldeagily bo done, if perfumed in the right manner. In the first place if men of standing in the town only considered the matter, especi illy the three Clergymen, whose congregations have the same with to act, wo should think, Cemetery, ought some energy. Let whoever has (or ought to have) the present in-pection, give it up, be they Policemas-

ter, Burgher Council or Grave -digger. A new Committee could then he chosen, which should dispose of the a courtyard-gang monthly, with view to and broad walks with gravel, the covering of the the planting of for sonic days trees to afford some little shade. Then grass ought not to be entirely destroyed would be left within proper bounds, which but should have a very good effect in this dry country, and it could be sold to the highest bidder, thereby rendering an important sum per annum, which should be appropriated to the beautyfying of said Churchyard. Tho transmitter of this is not aware if any one person lus the privilege of cutting the grass, should such be tho case, it is doubtless tli n the duty of the person to see that the churchyard is kept in proper order. The tombstones ought likewise to be. attended to, or they will be entirely demolished. If any one wishes to have a piece of ground for any length of time, say twenty years, it should be had for a certain sum, and alter the stated period had elapsed, renew the sum. The means of getting a handsome Churchyard are but trifling, all that is wanted, is a beginning, which must be gradual. CHRISTIANSTED, ST. CROIX. FRIDAY, 29th OCTOBER, 1S5S. At a meeting of the members of the St. Croix Athenaeum held ou Wednesday evening, a statement of its revenues and expenses was laid before them. It indicates, we are very sorry to say, a hopeless future for that institution. The largest item, which figured on the statement, was one of unpaid subscriptions ; arguing plainly' where the fault on fortunate, and reflects no credit lies. It is un- our community, that such an institution, want pretensions, cannot exist for with but humble of support. Like every other institution which administers to the requirements of the human mind, it lingers out a wretched existence for want of that attention which cannot be spared from the grosser pursuits of the sensual man. It would almost seem as if the object of existence in this place were to amass wealth, cat, drink, and die. Tho idea of wasting one dollar on the mind, does, we believe, appear to many as the height of folly. But the fault is not alone on the part of tho community. What eucouragement do die uthorities give to such institutions 1 Tho L islatuic of Barbadocs, displaying the common characteristic of all free countries, where the mental as well as physical man are the objects of solicitude on the part of their governments, not long since voted some hundred pounds Sterling for the purchase of books to add to the already large collection to at see We do not expect the public reading room. such example followed here : in fact, the idea would be scouted as tcdieulous, that either State or Latultreasury

should expend a cent for so unworthy an object! Nevertheless, we should like to bo informed, whether we shall ever hear of any public good being performed with the surplus of public revenue, apart from the lending ot money to our planters to purchase Com 51eal and Herrings. A Correspondent þÿiuto-day issue s points to the disgraceful condition of our Church Yard, which is purposely kept in grass-cultivation to be disposed of, we believe, for the benefit of the Landtreasury. There are other revenues derived from the Church Yard which are severely felt by those who have paid them ; that tho public a right to expect and which give it should be kept m decent order. Will not somo member of the Burgher Council gratify tho publio with a proposal to apply the surplus revenue to some useful purpose ! We shall not, we arc aware, learn of it until after the expiration of some months, when the proceedings arc published, but þÿ better late than þÿnever is a trite yet good old proverb.

A St. Petersburgh letter mentions the explosion of 1200 pouds (39,000 lb.) of gunpowder, which was undergoing tlie operation of being dried in the large powder manufactory of Okhta, about six miles from that capital. The Importance of Athletic Exkr cises. þÿ The gymnasium was quite as essential a portion of Greek education as the schoolroom, and the limbs of youths and even of grown men were as vigorously trained in athletic ex ercises as their brains in arithmetic, rhetoric, or philosophy. It was a wise and sound policy which led the ancients thus to value the bodily health and vigour that are to be gained by good physical training ; and the minds and frames of men now-a-days would be far healthier and their lives far happier if the same honour were now paid to skill and strength in physical exercises, and if the whole population were as care-: fully aided and encouraged in the pursuit of active sports as were the citizens of the Greek republics. Our contemporaries have, indeed, far more need of such physical education than the ancients had. The work of ancient days i is generally agricultural; men seldom were called upon to labour in-doors, and the toil of the farmer, or the hardships of the sailor and soldier, served to develope the limbs and strengthen the sinews of the race among whom the Olympic victors were held in honour. But, while men labour in close workshops or þÿill ventilated factories, and while children arc brought up to labour at the loom from the age of 9 or 10 years, we are almost utterly careless of the duty of providing them with proper means of bodily exercise and proper encouragement to use those means. We build schools for the young ; wo patronize þÿmechanics insti-

tutes for the adult. We provide books, stools, and desks to furnish the mind and accustom the body to sedentary habits. But we are little sedulous to supply our schools with playgrounds, or to furnish the working classes with healthful and strengthening recreations. The higher classes are better off. As youths, the emulation of the magnificent playgrounds of the great public schools initiates them into the love of cricket and football, and the universities teach them to boat and to ride. As men, they recreate themselves by tbc fatiguing sports of the Scotch moors or by the hearty exercise of tbc foxhunter. Yet too many of them, on leaving school, spend the remainder of tluir lives without exercise of any vigorous kind, and render themselves sickly and unhappy by the want of it. This mistake is a terrible one. Not only does it render the existing generation far inferior in strength and vigour to their hardy ancestors, but it impairs their health and transmits weakness aud suffering to their offspring. Indeed, considering how men now live, and remembering that women hardly ever enjoy any healthful bodily training whatsoever, it seems wonderful that the human race does not deteriorate faster than it actually seems to do in physical vigour and corporeal health. The necessity of bodily education ought to be, to any man possessed of common sense and an ordinary amount of physiological knowledge, at least as apparent as that of moral or intellectual training. Independently of the neces-

sity of bodily lie, iltb for its own sake no mind can be healthy or happy without it. It was recently said by a quaint but sensible divine that it is very difficult for a man with a bad to lie a good Christian ; and it is certainly far more difficult for him than for a man well trained in physical exertion and enjoying sound health to be a good citizen and a useful member of society. If these things were borne in mind by the philanthropists who are most laudably anxious for the education of the clas-

India Upper Court, the Royal þÿTreasurer s value of their benevolent labours would be more than doubled. In the present state of public knowledge and opinion it seems to us that more useful is the man who opens a gymnasium than he who endows a college ; more valuable he who lays out a playground than I he who builds a school. þÿ Manchester Guardian.

Mr. Editor ! As there are few owners of houses in town so well off but that they feci the ordinary taxes thereon a heavy burthen, and more especially, as these taxes in themselves must be considered entirely too high in proportion to the present value and revenue of the properties taxed, would it not beli >ve our representatives (if the Burgher Council, s it is composed, can bo said to represent the inhabitants of the towns) now, as the accounts of the Land Treasury show the same to be in a most flourishing condition, to exert themselves in order to have the taxes reduced and fixed ut a rate more suitable to the present times ? lfy accomplishing such a reduction the Burgher Council would confer a great boon on the owners of houses in straitened circumstances (alas ! by far the overwhelming majority,) and we would suppose, under these circumstances there can lie no great doubt but that the Honorable Board will do something towards the relief of the abovetnentioned class of their fellow-citizens. There is another item of taxation, which ought to come tinder the notice of our It prcsetitativos, with a view to a reduction in the same, I viz. the charges or fees for burgherbriefs or licenses They are generally speaking, fixed at a very high rate, comparatively, and sceui at the same time, in some instances evidently wrong in the principle. Thus, for instance : a person, having already taken out a burghersbrief as retailer, wishing to join to that establishment a sale of rum, must for that pur-

pose not only pay largely for a grant or licence; becomes not only subject to a perpetual tax, paid quarterly, as long as he retains the licence ; but is besides compelled to take out another burghersbri, f as rtiinshop-keepi r. Isi't this going to an extreme? It certainly seems trespassing on the bounds of on a just and equitable taxation, and bordering the system of mere money-making. Is not a similar remark applicable to that provision of the law, according to which burghcrbricls are to bo take.i out by persons being, or becoming, proprietors of sugar estates þÿ properties not only h -avily taxed directly, but also indirectly on the exportation of their produce J But suppose a sugar estate, devolving in some way or other to a person under age ; suppose a minor, a baby, becoming by inheritance proprietor ol such an estate, how then is this provision of the law to be carried into effect ? hunting to have been set on foot regard By the by, there seems of late in a regular to taking out burghcrbricfs and licences þÿ a complete razzia Many individuals who had, no doubt, thought themselves safely eusconced in the corner of oblivion, have been roused out of their sweet fancies by the peremptory call on their pockets : "betal!" Tito Landtreasury is unquestionably by fir the principal gainer of the fees charged on burgherbriefs. Vet while it is no more than right that what is fixed by law should be paid, also that the members of a community should defray the expenses of

the institutions established and upheld for their benefit and use, still when the community has accumulated upwards of $30,000, when such a sum is safe in the Landtreasury's chest, there is at any rate a strong probability that the members of the community pay more than what is required for defraying those expenses ; aud certainly, when such a probability exists, it seeins only a just claim on the part of the tax payers, that it be taken into consideration by their Representatives, the Members of the Burgher Council, whether, under such a state of things, some of the most onerous taxes might not be done away with. Yours, respectfully, A member of the community. Nov. 1, 1858.

We have on former occasions been witness to the ill effects of allowing the military to carry side-arms when not on duty, and in the last instance, which happened last evening, we cannot but wonder, from the many blows which we beard struck, that more serious injury bad not been inflicted, than those which a man received. It appears from what we could learn of the matter, that two soldiers, in a state of intoxication, got into some altercation with the keeper of one of our billiard rooms, Mr. Huyghue, and threatened to enforce their demands with their swords. This attracted a crowd of listeners by the steps ; seeing which, the soldiers became at once it tilled with military ardor and thought their duty to charge. They rushed on the crowd ; and the clank of their swords, intermingled with the cries of murder and lire, could be heard at some distance. One man received some severe cuts in the face, beyond which, we have not heard of the any unstea- injury being inflicted, through other diness, no doubt, of the soldiers' hands. A guard from the fort was soon dispatched by the Colonel and the men were placed immediately under arrest. We cannot hut make a remark on the danger to the lives of citizens which when useless practice of allowing soldiers, this not on duty, to carry arms, may at any moment give rise to. It is a question which we think ought to he settled between the military and civil authorities whether We practise should not be discontinued. the see no good effects arising from it ; but, on

the contrary much evil. We heard that one of the military authorities had put the very sapient question, " Why did not the by-standers take away the arms of the soldiers before they could use them?" Considering the strictness of the law in we ference to a citizeu's carrying arms, rethink the experiment would prove rather dangerous ; and we also think it a much easier way to settle the difficulty by keeping the arms in barracks and not to expect that the peaceful inhabitants should at any moment he ready to rush upon soldiers in a state of intoxication to disarm them. þÿ þÿ THE ST. In another portion of this sheet will be found reports of vessels that have arrived here within a few days in distress. All their commanders state, that very heavy gales had been expe-

rienced, and we learn that vessels have been spoken quite as disabled ; one somewhere in the neighbourhood of Sombrero from New York bound to this place, and said to be an English brig ; if so she will likely prove to he the Hibtrnia, which was reported to have left a week before the Vigilant schooner that arrived here sometime since. It is evident that very severe weather has been experienced along the Coasts of both North and South America, and that there will continue to arrive many more disabled vessels. The American schr. G M. Robertson, from Philadelphia, with dates to the 15th from that city, arrived here last evening; her commander states that ho encountered nothing hut a succession of gales throughout the voyage. We have been politely loaned a few papers brought by her. The Crystal Palace at New York had been burned down. It was leased to the American Institute for the purpose of holding in it its Annual Fairs, one of which was being held at the time the fire broke out, and is thought to have contained two thousand persons ; so rapidly did the flames increase that the mass escaped at considerable risk. Fortunately no lives iw re lost aud few persons injured. The amount of property destroyed is estimated at one million of dollars !

Boat Accident. The superb six-oared Gig belonging to Mr. C. J. Koefoed, was capsized or run over yesterday forenoon whilst boarding an American brigautine off the port, drowning one of the oarsmen. William Smith, and another, although rescued, is despaired of. The Gig, which must have received serious injury was towed to Buck Island, where she is now lying.

Arrived here on Thursday morning American ship Messenger, 460 tons, Captain ThomasTrott. She left New York on the 1st September for St. Cathrincs, (Brazil) with a cargo of coals for the United States Government. On the 21st September encountered a severe gale that continued to increase to the following day (S.'nd). At 3 p.m. lat. 33" N., long. 43" W., was forced to out away main and mizzen masts and run before the wind ; ship on her beam ends with cargo shifted ; four feet water in the hold and both pumps choked. Everything swept from the deck, boats included ; the pumps kept continually going, and for three days throwing coals overboard to lighten her in order to get the leak under. Met with the American barque Arabia, Capt. Washburn, of Fairhead, Mass., who kindly furnished Capt. Trott with a boat sufficiently large to have contained lite whole compliment of his ship, ard tor which act of kindness he expresses himself exceedingly grateful and returns Messrs. James <$- Philips.

(From the I Veekly Despatch. October 17.) THE BURNING OF THE AUSTRIA.

APPALLING DETAILS. By the Persia, which arrived at Liverpool on Sunday morning, we receive full details of tlio burning of the steam-ship Austria, of the Hamburg line of packets. As already stated 67 persons were rescued by the French barque Maurice. Twelve o! these were transferred to the barque Lotus, which arrived at Halifax on the 26th ult. Among these 12 was Mr. Ghartres Brew, the recently appointed inspector of police in British Columbia. The following narrative, furnished by Mr. Brew, appears in the New York Press : þÿ "I took passage at Southampton on the 4th Sept. in the steamship Austria, Captain Heydtmann, which left Hamburg on the 2nd. We sailed at 5 p.m., the evening being a little misty; we in consequence anchored between the Isle of Wight and the main land ; sailed again at 4 o'clock on the following morning. In weighing anchor an unfortunate accident occurred, by which one of the crew lost his life. Owing to some mismanagement the anchor ran out, whirling tho capstan round with terrific force, and hurling the men in all directions. Two were severely injured, and one thrown overboard, lie is supposed to have been instantly killed, as ho never rose to the surface. From the time the ship was laid on her course wo experienced strong westerly winds. On the 12th the weather was more favourable, and on the 1 3th a speed of 11 knots had been attained, and all were in

Ligh hopes of reaching New York by the 18th. At a little after 2 o'clock p.tn. I was on the quarter-deck. 1 saw a dense volume of smoke burst from the after entrance of the steerage. Some women ran aft, exclaimiug, ' The ship is on fire ! What will become of us !' The ship was instantly put at half speed, at which she continued until the magazine exploded, from which I infer the engineers were instantly suffocated. I only walked from where I was on the quarter-deck to the waist of the ship, when 1 Saw the flames breaking through the lights amidships. As the ship was head to the wind the fire travelled with fearful rapidity. I then went to the man at the wheel, and told him to put the vessel with her side to the wind. lie hesitated þÿ did not understand me, as he was a probably native of Hamburg. I then got a German gentleman to speak to him. At this time I saw some persons letting down the boat on the port side of the quarter-deck What became of the boat I don't know, but think she was crushed under the screw. I then went to let a boat over from the starboard side of the quarter-deck, but the moment we laid our hands on the ropes there were so many people who crowded into it that we could not lift it off the blocks. We therefore left it for a few minutes until the people got out, when we returned and launched it over the side of the ship, when, the people all rushing into it again, it descended with great violence into the water, and was instantly swamped, all the people being washed out ex-

cepting three, who held on to the sides. We then let down a rope and pulled up one person, who proved to bo the steward. Another, in the act, of being hauled up, was strangled by the rope. The fire now came on too fiercely to attempt to get up auy more from the swamped boat. All the. first cabin passengers were on the poop, with the exception of a few gentlemen, who must have been smothered in the smokingroom. .Many of the second cabin passengers were also on the poop, but a number of tbem got shut into their cabin by the fire. Some of them were pulled up through t lie ventilator, but the greater number could uot be extricated. T1 e last woman who was drawn up said there wei six already suffocated. We now perceived the the ship had got her head to the wind again, so that the flames came over the quarter-deck. In consequence of the crowd, 1 could not get to the wheelliouse to ascertain the reason, but I was informed that the helmsman had deserted his p ist, and that the vessel, being left to herself, headed to the wind of her own accord. At this time the scene on the quarter-deck was indescribable and truly heartrending Passengers were rushing frantically to and fro þÿ husbands seeking their wives, wives in search of their husbands, relatives looking after relatives, mothers lamenting the loss of their children, some wholly paralysed by fear, others madly crying to he saved ; hut a few perfectly calm and collected. The flames pressed so closely upon them that many jumped into the sea; relatives,

clasped in each others' arms, leaped over and met a watery grave ; two girls supposed to ho sisters, jumped over and sank kissing each other. A missionary and wife leaped into the sea together, and the stewardess and assistant steward, arm in arm, followed. One Hungarian geutlernan, with seven fine children, four of them girls, children, made tbem jump in one after the oi lie made his wife jump in, then blessed his six eld- at , and followed them with an infant in his own arms. I, about this tiinc, was standi ig outside the bulwarks, holding on by the davits, loaning out to avoid the flames, which were leaping towards me. I saw a swamped boat, under me, spinuiug by a rope, still attached to the ship; as the oars were tied in her, 1 thought if 1 could got to her I would be enabled to save myself and others. I let myself down by a rope, passing over a man who was clinging to it but who refused to come with inc. I took out a penknifo to cut the tackle ; the large blade broke, and I then severed it with the small blade. The ship passed ahead. As the screw approached I found the boat drawn towards it. I tried to keep the boat off, but the screw caught and capsized her over me. I dived away from the ship and came to the surface near a boat which was keel upwards ; I got on her, and by pressing on one side, with the assistance of a wave she righted, but was still swamped. The oars had been knocked out by the screw ; the only thing I could find in her to paddle with was some laths
nailed together as a sheathiDg for the sides. I When I looked around (be ship was a quarter of

S; T'« C R 0 I X AVIS , a miie away from me. I could see the ladies and gentlemen jumping off the poop into the wa iu twos and three s, some of the ladies in flames. Several h ituud to leap from the burning ship until e last moment, as the height was 22 feet, and were only at length compelled to throw themselves off to avoid a more painful death. In half an hour not a soul was to be seen on the poop. 1 pulled after the ship and picked up a German who was swimming strongly ; 1 got him beside me on the boat, and we paddled alter the ship with th« laths. 1 "now saw a vessel under sail approaching -y shoncached the steamer about 5 p.m.; we, continued pulling towards them, and about half-past 7 o'clock, after being five hours iu the w#tor, got withiu bail of the sailing vessel, which put off a boat and took us on board. She proved to be the French barque Mauriue, Capt. Ernest Rcnaud, of Nantes, bound from Newfoundland for Isle of Bourbon, with fish. She had, up to that time, rescued 40 passengers of the burning steamer, chiefly taken off the bowsprit, though a few were picked up floating around. At about 8 o'clock ouc of the metallic boats came up with about 32 persons, includiug the first and third officers ; afterwards three or four men were picked up, floating on a piece of tko broken boat. The second officer was taken up, having been swimming, with nothing The second i ' i!. d officers were severely to float him, for six hours. burned; one male nger was burned frightfully, and some oti > There were but t m s u d, three of whom - !e p isscDgers slightly.

were burned iu . -U.< ;ii inner. " Captain R i ud a suili the utmost kindness. lie gave i as fa. as he could furnish them t. tlio sin g passengers, and acted as nurse, doctoi and irg on to the burned people, dressing the wounds of the females with a delicacy and tenderness that evinced a benevolent aud amiable disposition. " I did not sec an officer of the ship during the fire, aud am certain there was not one of them or the crew on the poop, except a man at the wheel for a short time. I understood that win e captain hcui 1 ol the fire, he rushed on deck ou a I at, which, when let down, was swamped, claimed, - . 'Ut a cap, and when he saw the flames, ' We arc all 1 ist.' He tried to get and he, whether accidentally or not I do not know, fell into the so . or, I was soon left far hehind. The foutth officer was in this boat. He cut her loose in m the davits; she was carried under the screw and smashed, n 1 several in i,er drowned. Three or four men « cap d i aim ment, aud were picked up by the V . before stated. About the same time on ,n. tallic life-boat was let dowu from the port now aud swamped, but got cleared away with about 33 persons in her, including the first and third officers and several women. The men in this boat capsized her two or three times in trying to clear her of water. Ten persons were thus drowned, including some women. They afterwards bailed her out with life preservers cut in two, and pulled to the Maurice, having (ickcd up two or three passengers before reaching tho barque.

Altogether there were li7 souls taken into the Maurice during the night. " A Norwegian barque came up with the steamer the next morning, and a boat was observed going around the burning ship. They may have picked up a few persons, but only a very few. At about 7 o'clock the Maurice sailed for Fayal to deposit the rescued passengers. At about 2 o'clock the same afternoon she fell in with the barque Lotus, Captain Trefy, of Yarmouth, Nova Scotia, from Liverpool for Halifax. As I was anxious to get on British territory, Captain Trcfy kindly gave me passage. He was also anxious to take all the American citizens, but there was such a rush of foreigners into the boats that only one load of 1 1 could be got off, " and even several of these were foreigners. The fire is known to have arisen from very culpable negligence of some of the crew. The captain and surgeon considered it expedient to fumigate the steerage with burning tar. Tho operation was to be performed by the boatswain, under the superintendence of the fourth officer. The boatswain heated the end of a chain to dip in tar to produce stnokc. The end became too hot to hold, and ho let it drop upon the deck, to which it set firo. The tar upset and immediately all about was in flames. A feeblo attempt was made to extinguish it, but without effect. There was nothing at hand to meet such an emergency. The rcscuod passengers saved nothing hut the clothes on their backs, and even the greater part
of these were torn off and otherwise lost. Six hundred souls were supposed to be on board including many women and children." Mr. Brew is the ODly British subject saved.
